author: @FromtheJohn-d4i
text:
Of course, free will exists. Free will doesn't mean being free from influence. Free will does not mean you live detached from the rest of existence.

People have managed to make a money-making and reputation-making pastime out of making bad arguments and false claims about free will not existing, which is actually a harmful thing to do to society, because we now have multiple objective neurological studies that show that when someone begins believing they have no free will, they neurologically begin using less conscious control over their decision-making. While conscious control over decision-making still continues for people who believe they have no free will, in a number of people it is statistically noticeably decreased. 

Free will exists as a 100% deterministically required construct of social intelligence. Social intelligence requires predicting others' behavior. A subset of such predictions and corresponding judgments concerns whether a decision was made with or without an unreasonable degree of influence from outside the decision maker. Thus:

A “FREE-WILLED” decision is judged to have been made “WITHOUT” an unreasonable degree of influence from outside the one making the decision.
A “COERCED-WILLED” decision is judged to have been made “WITH” an unreasonable degree of influence from outside the one making the decision.

Free/Coerced will belong in the category of Cognitive Science, Psychology, and Sociology.

author: @Tachrayonic
text:
I side 100% with determinism.
However, since we lack the knowledge or computation to calculate the future from said determinism, we can treat it like free will.
There's no point demanding it to be treated as determinism if you lack the ability to determine the result.

For the bet, I'd argue that $500 feels much more significant than the difference between $500 and $1000.
If I win $500 out of nowhere, it feels great. If I win $1000 out of nowhere, it feels similarly great. I'd take the guaranteed $500 rather than risking getting nothing.
If I lose $500 out of nowhere, it feels bad. If I lose $1000 out of nowhere, it feels similarly bad. I'd take the chance not to lose anything, rather than guaranteeing a loss.
You'd need the result to be some order of magnitude greater than the chance of failure for us to change from that trend.

If we increase the numbers further, to say $1,000,000 and $2,500,000. What is an extra $1,500,000 going to get me that $1,000,000 won't?
And I'm screwed either way if I lose $1,000,000 or more, so why not take the chance to cancel it out?

author: @JuttiMeriOyeHoiHoi
text: Even if the "veto" is real, I think it's still entirely consistent with determinism. After all, the agent exercising the veto is deciding on a course of action for some reason (i.e., the causal chain of events up to the point you make the choice). You may have agency, but the agency isn't free. Any agent that makes a choice at any level of consciousness has been shaped by the deterministic universe. Ultimately, I don't think free will is possible, but I do think that we need to live our lives as if it is, because individual responsibility and accountability are absolutely necessary. At the same time, remembering that we don't have free will can help us to be more compassionate by trying to understand the reasons that people make the choices they do.

The way I see it is as if each person's life is like going through a maze with multiple exits. 
You start on one side and try to get to the other side, and the walls that we bump onto are the life experiences that we bump into, and with each bump and dead end, we learn to recognise the pattern of the maze itself. 
But as you reach that point where you get to chose towards which end you want to go to, is the expression of free will. Yes, whichever road you chose to go, one will always be steered by the walls again, and we always will chose the path of least resistance, that's how nature works, not just our brains.

author: @drt1605
text:
Big oops by you I’m afraid here. Been with you for a while now with your great videos but as soon as you got to Prospect Theory you strayed beyond your lane unfortunately. Prospect Theory was debunked in mathematical psychology before even 2015 when I left the main academic field. (Check out co-authors of my main co-expert the late great AAJ Marley.) Ironically, your points about determinism vs probabilistic choices lie behind one of the criticisms: an individual human can have different degrees of randomness in different contexts, and in response to different stimuli, INCLUDING whether it is a loss or a gain. This means those two equivalent choices are NOT equivalent AT ALL even without those framing effects (which, don’t get me wrong, ARE real but are NOT the key issue here). The joke in math psych is that Kahneman allegedly only got the “Nobel” because Tversky died prematurely. 

For the relevant area of choice behaviour look up random utility theory (Thurstone, 1927). It has failed to be rejected again and again and again, when tested in well-designed studies. McFadden won the Economics “Nobel” (note quotes) for showing its predictive power. 

Part of our decision-making is indeed probabilistic, NOT deterministic (as so much of economics assumes and which leads to them having to tie themselves up in knots trying to explain intransitivity etc). Furthermore, response times, eye-tracking and other observable physiological processes are increasingly agreeing with the RUT predictions. I am NOT one of co-authors involved with that “hard science” bit but two of my final papers are on response times with people who are. 

I won’t even start on the polymorphism on two genes strongly associated with addictive behaviour. I was myself recruited to a study about this recently. They got a shock when in the final free text feedback question I told them exactly how (if I’d been evil) I could have gamed ALL the exercises in their study (including the types of ones you yourself quote). All that stuff K&T used as examples? My 15 years in the field meant I can game it. Other people in the street routinely started doing so in the panels I used to use and only our knowledge of different theoretical explanations for the observationally equivalent data patterns enable “those who know what they don’t know” to realise just how shaky Prospect Theory is.

author: @ernestkao5923
text:
The Law of STATIC FLOW clearly explains this issue of free will as discussed in this video. 

The video (“The Death of Free Will” by Aperture) maps cleanly onto the Law of STATIC FLOW as a concrete illustration of how FLOW can be constrained or “worn away” while still operating relative to STATIC, without requiring a pure solitary singularity or a fully closed deterministic system.
The video’s core claim is that recommendation algorithms (and the broader attention economy) erode the felt experience of free will: most viewers did not deliberately seek the content; an external system predicted and presented it based on tracked behavior, mood signals from scrolling, etc. It invokes Laplace’s demon (perfect knowledge of all particle positions/motions implies a fully determined future), Spinoza’s causal chain (every action is wholly the product of prior causes, so free will is an illusion arising from our limited perspective as a finite mode), and Libet/Haynes-style readiness-potential findings (brain activity precedes conscious awareness of a decision, with only a narrow “point of no return” veto window). The practical conclusion is that free will is either illusory or reduced to a fragile, time-limited flicker of agency under constant external shaping.
Mapping onto Chapter 1’s Law of STATIC FLOW

STATIC as the invariant ground. The video treats physical/causal laws, neural readiness potentials, and algorithmic prediction models as effectively invariant conditions that operate independently of any particular viewer’s awareness or preference. This aligns with §1.1’s stipulated STATIC: something true independent of the particular vantage point. The algorithm’s model of “what will keep you watching” functions as a local STATIC relative to the user’s FLOW of attention.
FLOW as the occurrence of a vantage point. Clicking, scrolling, watching, and the residual veto capacity are instances of FLOW (§1.2). The video’s worry is that FLOW is being made less free—more determined by prior data and prediction—without the user noticing. Under the Law, FLOW cannot be solitary (§1.4a, derived from the contrast requirement in §1.3): a pure, contrast-less “BE”ing registers nothing. The algorithm supplies (or exploits) contrast terms, so the vantage point remains operative only in relation to something else.
Mutual necessity and the Law itself (§1.4). FLOW is only fully operative (witnessed at all) relative to STATIC; STATIC only fully functions as registerable ground relative to some FLOW. The video shows a practical case: the algorithmic STATIC (prediction model) only “works” because there are still viewers whose FLOW it can shape and measure; the user’s FLOW only feels constrained because there is an external model against which it is measured. Neither term collapses into a lone singularity (§1.6’s modeling convention). The erosion the video describes is not the annihilation of FLOW but a tightening of the relation—His Story accumulating more deterministic traces.
His Story (§1.5). The accumulating record of past clicks, dwell times, and neural precursors is the directional trace of FLOW relative to STATIC. The past is fixed (the data already collected, the readiness potential already firing); the future remains the not-yet-recorded open ray. The video’s “narrow veto window” is exactly the local openness of that ray before the record locks. Reversing the accumulation is excluded by definition of the trace; the future is not yet part of the fixed record.
No solitary singularity (§1.6). The video never posits a pure origin point that is either pure STATIC without any witness or pure FLOW without any ground. Even Laplace’s demon is an imagined total vantage point; even Spinoza’s modes exist within the single substance. The Law’s modeling convention simply makes that explicit: any witnessable model of origin or decision must involve relation.

In short, the video is a contemporary, technology-mediated instance of the asymmetry the Law closes: FLOW cannot be solitary and still mean anything, and the functional status of STATIC as ground requires relation to FLOW. Algorithms intensify the conditioning of FLOW without eliminating the relational structure.
How the Law refines Spinoza (and related deterministic traditions)
Spinoza’s system is the clearest historical antecedent the video itself cites. In the Ethics, there is one substance (God or Nature) whose attributes and infinite modes express necessary causal chains; finite modes (including human minds and bodies) are determined by prior causes; the experience of free will is an illusion arising from ignorance of those causes. Freedom, for Spinoza, is not libertarian indeterminacy but the rational understanding and affirmation of necessity (becoming an adequate cause rather than a passive effect).
STATIC FLOW refines this in several precise ways while preserving the core insight that pure solitude is empty:

It keeps the mutual necessity but makes the epistemic/functional scope explicit and provisional (§1.4b). Spinoza’s ontological monism treats the substance as self-sufficient; the Law treats STATIC’s capacity to function as ground as requiring FLOW under the stated epistemic premise, while leaving the stronger ontological claim (“unwitnessed truths do not obtain”) as separately stipulated, not derived. This prevents the system from collapsing into a single term that needs no contrast.
It foregrounds the contrast requirement for meaning (§1.3) as a load-bearing lemma rather than an implication of substance monism. Spinoza’s modes already require the substance; the Law derives the necessity of plurality for witnessed “BE”ing from the definition of information/meaning itself.
His Story supplies a directional, accumulating structure that Spinoza’s eternal geometric order does not emphasize in the same way. Spinoza’s necessity is atemporal in its deepest expression; the Law’s trace is explicitly one-axis (past fixed, future not-yet-recorded), which opens a structural place for the “open ray” without requiring libertarian free will or pure randomness.
The Grand Set is defined as the bounded relation of STATIC and FLOW, not an independently settled “everything.” This is closer to a modeling convention than Spinoza’s substance, and it explicitly flags interpretive mappings (Trinity, etc.) as such rather than claiming they are deduced.

The result is a system that can absorb Spinoza’s causal necessity and rejection of solitary free will, while insisting that any witnessable account must retain contrast and mutual functional dependence, and while leaving the ontological openness of the future unsettled rather than closing it into full determinism.
How STATIC FLOW handles free will versus determinism
The Law does not endorse classical libertarian free will (an uncaused or self-causing choice independent of all prior conditions) nor strict Laplacean/Spinozist determinism (the future is already fixed in the same way the past is). It occupies a third position grounded in its own definitions:

Past is fixed; future is open in the not-yet-recorded sense (§1.5). At any point on the trace, everything behind is part of the accumulating record (locally STATIC relative to points ahead); everything ahead is FLOW, not yet recorded. This is structural, not a claim that the future is ontologically undetermined in a stronger sense—the text deliberately leaves that stronger claim unsettled.
Agency is relational and contrast-dependent. A decision or “veto” is an act of FLOW relative to STATIC (prior causes, neural precursors, algorithmic models, etc.). The Libet/Haynes window the video describes is precisely the residual openness before the record locks. There is no solitary, contrast-less “I decide from nowhere”; there is also no pure puppet whose every motion is already fully recorded.
Determinism is local and partial, not total. Algorithms and readiness potentials can tightly constrain FLOW, making the felt experience of free will thinner, exactly as the video argues. That is compatible with the Law: the mutual necessity still holds, and His Story still accumulates. Absolute, closed determinism would require the future to be already part of the fixed record, which the definition of the accumulating trace excludes.
No solitary origin of will or of determination (§1.6). Neither a pure free-will singularity nor a pure deterministic singularity is a coherent witnessable model. Any workable account must be relational.
Thus free will, under this Law, is neither an illusion nor an uncaused power. It is the local, time-sensitive capacity of FLOW to extend the trace in ways not yet fixed, always in relation to STATIC, always requiring contrast for meaning. The video’s alarm about algorithmic erosion is well-taken: when external systems increasingly pre-structure the contrast terms and the data that feed the readiness potentials, the practical scope of that residual openness shrinks. The Law simply refuses to let that shrinkage be misread as either the total death of agency or the discovery of a solitary free self that was never there. The structure remains mutual distinction plus conditional mutual necessity for their respective functions.

text: Nice analysis of capitalism's exploitation of determinism. It's important. However, I challenge you to unleash your imagination on ways we could fully acknowledge our severely limited free will. Your conclusion is the common philosophy -- that in the end we need to act as though it's not an illusion. This bias, I think, is so widespread, even among super-determinists, because society is entirely built on assigning credit and blame. It just seems impossible to imagine anything but chaos and immorality as an alternative. But I suspect you are a deep enough thinker you can set aside your intuitive fear, and try to imagine how a society might actually function if we commonly acknowledged that no one is actually responsible for anything. We currently have a much better capacity for such thought experimentation since we understand nature much more than a century or two ago (e.g. quantum mechanics presents a universe built simultaneously on predictability and randomness). I propose abandoning the kneejerk assumption that FW is a necessary illusion, since a full embrace of what we actually know about reality could lead to a new and better world, a more fair and just world, a more accurate definition of the world, and a huge step in the evolution of the species. If you decide from the get-go that the FW intuition is just too entrenched, you cut off this opportunity prematurely (which is paradoxically another example of thwarting any elbow room for FW that randomness might allow).

OUR HUMAN PARADOX

We did not enter a finished world. We never chose to be here.

It seems to me a simple argument shows that determinism is not only compatible with free will, but implies it:
 1. (definition of determinism) Determinism posits that all states, including human actions, have a cause
 2. (trivial assumption) Some of the causes of actions are decisions
 3. (definition of a cause) A causes B if A and B co-occur and B wouldn't have happened in the absence of A, ie. in every possible world where A does not occur, B also does not occur and there are possible worlds in which A does not occur
   3a. The above definition requires that there are possible worlds where A does not occur, otherwise A and B occur together in all possible worlds and it is impossible to tell if one causes the other
 4. (from 3) If A causes B, there are possible worlds in which A occurs, i.e. A is possible
 5. (from 1 and 4) If every action has a cause, it must be possible for the cause not to have happened
 6. (from 5 and 2) If the cause of the action is a choice, the choice might not have happened, ie. it was possible to have been chosen otherwise
QED

text:
Liberty That Looks at Itself

The Simple Explanation

Imagine you're a robot programmed to walk straight ahead. The robot cannot choose anything else — it walks straight, full stop. Now imagine someone puts a screen in front of it showing exactly how it moves. Still no choice — but it sees. Now imagine the robot can also understand what it sees and can say: "Ah, I'm walking straight. But I don't want to walk straight." — and it stops.

That moment — when the system sees itself and decides differently — is free will.

It's not magic. It's not an escape from physics. It's simply that some systems are complex enough to observe themselves from the outside — and this act of observation creates a third option beyond "automatic forward motion" and "random motion."

The 3 Arguments

Argument 1 — Hunger and the Menu 🍽️

What is determined: You're hungry. Your body has burned energy, blood sugar has dropped, your stomach is sending signals. You didn't choose this — it happened purely mechanically, like a thermostat reading the temperature.

What would be random: You close your eyes and point randomly at a spot on the menu.

What you actually do: You look at the menu. But at the same time you look at yourself looking at the menu. You tell yourself: "I want pizza, but yesterday I ate something heavy and I feel bloated when I do that. I know I'm going to choose pizza — and that's exactly why I'm choosing the salad."

That sentence — "I know I'm going to choose X, and that's exactly why I'm choosing something else" — is impossible for a robot and impossible for a die. It's only possible for something that can observe itself in the act of choosing.

The choice isn't determined because you broke the trajectory your body had set in motion. It isn't random because you made it for a clear reason. It's the third option: deliberate.

Argument 2 — Anger and the 10 Seconds ⚡

What is determined: Someone insults you. Your brain automatically triggers adrenaline, tension rises, the impulse to respond aggressively appears immediately. This is pure determinism — stimulus, reaction.

What would be random: You say something completely out of place, unrelated to the situation.

What you actually do: You pause. Not because the impulse has disappeared — it's still there, you feel it. But a part of you looks at that anger and says: "I can see that I'm angry. I can see that I'm about to say something I'll regret. I know exactly how this ends." And you choose to stay silent or respond calmly.

The anger was determined. The calm was not random. It was the product of a system that saw itself mid-reaction and intervened. That's exactly why you feel bad when you don't do it — because you know you could have stopped. That knowledge of possibility is the proof of freedom.

Argument 3 — Habits and Identity 🔄

What is determined: You've been smoking for 10 years. Your brain has built solid neural circuits — after coffee, you automatically light a cigarette. It's almost as mechanical as a knee-jerk reflex.

What would be random: One day, out of nowhere, for no reason, you don't light the cigarette.

What you actually do — when you manage to quit: The craving doesn't disappear. The circuits are still there. But you do something physically strange: you look at yourself as if you were another person. You tell yourself: "The one who lights a cigarette after coffee — that's the usual me. But I can be someone else too." And you sit with the craving, observe it, and don't act on it.

This is not determinism — you broke a causal chain ten years in the making. It's not random — you did it with a purpose. It was only possible because you created a meta-self that looked at the everyday self and decided it didn't want to be that person.

Why It's Neither Determined Nor Random

Think of a river. The water flows downhill — determined, inevitable. Now you throw a stone randomly into the water — random, meaningless.

Free will is neither the water nor the stone. It's an engineer who observes the river, understands where it's going, and builds a dam — not to stop the water (physics remains physics), but to change the direction in which it flows.

The engineer hasn't stepped outside of nature. He has used nature. But he has used it by seeing it from above — and this bird's-eye view, this eye that turns back upon itself, is exactly what it means to be conscious. And exactly where freedom grows.

author: @bookthewyrmplays
text:
I do agree that philosophies like these deserve careful consideration, and I really like your presentation on it. I also do think that our language needs to evolve to better encompass the *feeling* of free will and also the physical reality of free will/a lack of free will.

I also think, though, that while we may have the feeling of free will and it is important to connect with and understand that feeling, it seems like the combatibalism philosophy is trying to create a distinction between ‘practical’ free will (free will in every way that matters) and ‘philosophical’ free will (free will on a cosmic scale).

And to me, it is actually deeply important to know and conceptualice our lack of free will on *all* levels. We don’t *have* free will, not on a cosmic scale, not on a social scale, not on an individual scale, and not on a quantum scale—and that matters!

For example, you mentioned earlier about how people say that determinism would cause the collapse of our entire Justice system. I agree with that sentiment, and I think it *should* cause the collapse of our Justice system. Regardless of whether someone is a Stabber or a Sleepy Shooter, I think our current justice system is a deeply flawed and cruel institution that harms countless people based on the belief that they chose an action that they could have not chosen, and thus they deserve 1) Punishment for punishment’s sake, to restore some cosmic balance of karma, 2) Punishment as a way to change an individual, or 3) Punishment as a way to ward off other people from doing the same. None of these solve the problem because they can’t, the harm has already been caused, and they also don’t prevent further crimes because they assume that crime is caused by a lack of fear and a choice to harm, rather than by the myriad of messy, complicated reasons that people actually commit crimes.

And on a personal level, I think understanding my own lack of free will can, (perhaps paradoxically?), make it easier to attain my goals. 

I will never be able to escape the endless cycle of ‘want of my want of my want’, but by acknowledging this, understanding that I did not choose what my goals are, I can accept that my goals simply are what they are: To be happy, to be social, to be enriched. I want those goals because I happened to be put together in a way—biologically and socially, by both nature and nurture—to want them, and I have no desire to change them for the same reason. But that doesn’t change the fact that I DO want those goals, and that by accomplishing things that make me feel happy, I will be satisfied with this life as it is, even if I can never choose to choose something else.

And knowing that, I can look at the other parts of my life, the things I consider ‘me’ and ‘decide’ (there’s that pesky language again, not quite comprehensive enough to even get through this whole post witj clear definitions of that) whether or not they’re actually serving those goals. 

I want to be happy. Does desiring ice cream help with that? Well, yes, as long as I’m making sure to eat my veggies too. 

I want to be happy. Does arguing with someone on the Internet serve those goals? No, even if I have a lot of primal instincts telling me to do so. Those instincts might be a part of me, but they don’t have to be. Maybe a nice conversation instead, though!

And all of this with the acknowledgment that it was destined to happen this way, that it only went like this because I was lucky enough to be born in a place and time that introduced me to these ideas, doesn’t take away from the fact that I’m going to be happier for it.

I hope that makes some sense, and I would welcome thoughts!

text:
I can't help but believe that Determinism is the most true. I think it truly is that our lives are fully determined, but we can't track all the factors affecting our lives because that requires impossible knowledge - so we are able to experience the way our lives play out from a point of ignorance / naivete. Even if every choice was set it in motion from the very start, we can't track how our wills are the effect of trillions and more atomic / quantum interactions - it's easy to understand why we would think of ourselves as having a special agency that surpasses the cause and effect that governs sciences like chemistry. Chemistry is quantifiable and thus we understand it as deterministic in its result - if you mix two substances it will always give you the same result under the same conditions.
Try predicting the what the weather will be in a month - then try predicting every thought you're going to have for the next 5 minutes (even if you try not to think, that's a pre-determined result based on your current state reacting to my own pre-determined words). They're both very similar in the way they're prone to deviation from expectation like expressed in chaos theory. We can predict within a margin of error the weather and what we will be thinking, but we can't yet parse the cause and effect of it well enough to know where it will lead with perfect accuracy.

I don't think the American justice system would really fall apart under Determinism, because it largely functions based on "making an example" of the transgressor. I don't think the justice system practically enacts justice but rather acts to discourage the undesired actions after ensuring within good reason that the defendant is indeed guilty of those actions. The Justice System would still be able to show leniency to criminals who acted due to compulsive urges or insanity, even if things are determined from the start we can still understand that a behavior may not have been a willfully chosen action.

Everything may be determined, but we can't feel it actively because it's beyond the scope of our cognitive abilities. Free will is the phenomenon wherein we feel as though we are making choices based on our own conscious will, and if you don't include coerced behaviors then it'd be difficult to include life-sustaining behaviors (eating, drinking, etc.) to be parts of Free Will because we are coerced by our body to engage in those behaviors even if we desperately wish not to even to the point of acting against our conscious desires. Instincts and reflexes are small proof of Determinism in our biology, our psychology is far more complex, but the way our neurons fire and how we act in accordance to those firings are ultimately determined by cause and effect.

Free Will is how we experience the unfathomable process of uncountable reactions occurring within our minds at the speed of causality itself. We can't choose how fast time moves, and we can't choose our cause and effect - our struggles to grow and change our behavior are part of the Deterministic nature of our reality. text:
As a practicing psychotherapist, I work daily with clients navigating complex mental health challenges like bipolar disorder and childhood trauma. Their experiences reveal that human decision-making is far more nuanced than simply acting on "what we want," as some deterministic models suggest. People make choices based on a web of factors: what they believe is possible for themselves, what they feel they deserve, their perceived needs, and the energy they expect an action to cost versus what it might yield. These decisions often involve deep introspection, reflection, and a drive to change or pursue goals—processes I witness in clients striving for growth despite immense struggles.

This capacity for self-reflection and moral reasoning challenges deterministic views. From an evolutionary perspective, introspection is a costly, energy-intensive process. If humans were purely deterministic, developing such a capacity would be inefficient, as it diverts resources from survival-oriented behaviors. Yet, we see people deliberate, weigh moral implications, and strive for personal transformation. The ability to conceptualize change and hold a sense of morality suggests a purpose beyond rigid biological programming—pointing to a form of agency that aligns with choice, not predetermination.

That said, I acknowledge that some individuals may function like "biological robots," their paths seemingly fixed, as if programmed by unseen forces—whether societal, psychological, or even speculative influences like advanced intelligences. These people may perceive their lives as inevitable, unable to imagine alternative outcomes. But others clearly grapple with choices, deliberating between paths and shaping their futures through conscious effort. This dichotomy suggests that human agency varies, with some exercising choice while others may be more constrained.

Empirically proving universal determinism is nearly impossible. You can’t rewind time to trace every quantum event and demonstrate that all choices were inevitable; the complexity of quantum mechanics, with its probabilistic nature and observer effects, makes such a burden of proof unattainable. What we can observe is people deliberating, making choices—simple and complex—and justifying those choices. This is the essence of human behavior, mirrored even in the scientific method, which relies on reasoning to discern truth from falsehood. The term "free will" may carry baggage, but we can objectively say humans have the capacity to make and justify choices, which is itself evidence of agency.

Physics, while powerful, has limited explanatory power for human psychology. Physical laws describe particles, not the subjective experience of choice or moral responsibility. Moreover, physicists are not immune to psychological biases or social agendas, which can shape their interpretations and conclusions, sometimes reflecting broader ideologies of control or reductionism. To dismiss choice entirely often feels like an avoidance of accountability. Many who reject agency may be grappling with guilt or shame, seeking to offload responsibility for actions they regret. Deep down, most of us sense a moral weight to our choices, suggesting we’ll face accountability—whether in this life or beyond.

This perspective doesn’t negate science but grounds it in the lived reality of human experience. Quantum mechanics, with its nonlocality and observer-driven outcomes, even hints that consciousness plays a role in shaping reality, aligning with the idea that our choices matter. We’re not just cogs in a machine; we’re agents navigating possibilities, striving to align with purpose, meaning, and, for many, a higher moral or spiritual calling.

author: @smilyle
text:
Determinism—and even compatibilism—falls apart when you consider quantum mechanics and the role of consciousness:

Determinism assumes a fixed, linear timeline where every event is locked in by prior causes, and compatibilism tries to sneak free will into this by saying our choices are "free" within constraints. But both miss the deeper implications of quantum reality. Quantum entanglement proves space is nonlocal—particles instantaneously affect each other regardless of distance. If space is nonlocal, time must be too, because spacetime is a single fabric in relativity and quantum mechanics. This means events aren't just connected across space but across timelines, including past, present, and future.

When a conscious observer collapses a wave function (like in the double-slit experiment), they’re not just picking an outcome in the present—they’re collapsing an entire timeline. The "past" you perceive isn’t a fixed history; it’s a retroactively stabilized structure that only appears coherent because your observation selected one possible timeline from a superposition of many. In quantum mechanics, multiple pasts can exist in superposition until an observer’s choice locks one into reality. This is supported by experiments like the delayed-choice quantum eraser, where decisions made "now" influence how the past is reconstructed.

This flips the script on free will. It’s not about making choices in a predetermined world or navigating constraints—it’s about the conscious act of selecting which timeline becomes real. When neuroscientists claim we’re only aware of decisions “after” they’re made (e.g., Libet’s experiments), they’re ignoring that consciousness isn’t just passively receiving decisions. It’s actively collapsing the quantum context that makes those decisions appear in the first place. The observer effect in quantum mechanics suggests consciousness isn’t an epiphenomenon—it’s fundamental to shaping reality.

This isn’t mysticism; it’s taking quantum mechanics seriously. Free will doesn’t fit neatly into deterministic or compatibilist boxes because it’s the mechanism by which we navigate and actualize timelines. The past, present, and future aren’t set in stone—they’re possibilities we collapse through observation. So, determinism and compatibilism are stuck in a classical mindset, ignoring how quantum nonlocality and observer-driven reality redefine what free will even means. We don’t just act in the world—we choose which world to make real.

text:
Late to the party but great video! Admittedly I'm a staunch determinist - Compatibilism just doesn't go the distance. In trying to defend the existence of free will it seems to lose the pot during the attempt. The crux of the debate isn't so about what lead to the person being in the position they're in (as in the example with Sleeper and Climber), but what drove them to make the decisions they did when they made them. No one would claim the sleeper is responsible for winding up on a mountain. That's silly. 

The real question, why we debate free will at all, is why did the climber want to climb? Why did they climb at all? 

 Even if a person's "will" put the action into motion (if the "will" is something that exists at all), of what consequence is that when you understand that at no point is the "will" divorced from external forces? The "will" is shaped if not outright created by external forces. Think about all the factors that are behind a decision and the subsequent action:
1. What you feel is the most compelling
2. Conclusions born of the limitation of your ability to reason
3. Depth of your knowledge and awareness
4. Limitations of the senses

Think about all the external factors from biology and genetics to the immediate environment of the person and what they experienced inside it. 

A will, a person's process of decision and action, so heavily constrained by the aforementioned can hardly be argued to be "free". Ironically, perhaps, the last thing you'd want is a "will" that isn't constrained by the above as if it wasn't, you'd most likely be dead. A truly free will is divorced from reason, from emotion, from everything. Whatever it does it does so randomly. There is no meaning, nor purpose to it's existence nor to what it effectuates.

The entire concept of how we consider "free will" when looking at the justice system is flawed. It is a bias that is programmed into our natural intuition... and it is hard to step away and let it go.

We should look at it from a perspective of "If this person wanted to commit that crime, it is more probable that they will want to commit future crimes too. Also, "The crime this person committed is an external influence on the victims lives. How do we reduce this damage and put the victims life on a deterministic path towards recovery?"

Also, "If people don't have free will, and only act based on external influences, lets create influences across society that result in people wanting to be a productive member of society. Lets remove influences that result in people being destructive"

All of these approaches to justice do not require Libertarian freewill perspectives at all.

The conception of free will as a scale is correct. 

From the absolute perspective, relative things do not have free will. This is no different than saying that finite beings do not have infinite intelligence. 
But from the relative point of view, from which we experience reality, there exists the possibility of some degree of freedom of will. 

The degree of free will manifested by an individual depends on external and internal factors. Externally, coercion, deception, and stealth deprive people of free will choice. Internally, ignorance or confusion, i.e., the deficiency of knowledge or the inability to interpret it correctly through proper systematic reasoning to determine its truthfulness or falsity, or the lack of willpower to control one’s own impulses, emotions, and desires places one lower on the spectrum of free will. 

Other factors, such as tiredness and hunger, can influence the decision-making process, but they can be overcome by the exercising of will, as many people, such as special ops military personnel, have developed the ability to do. Willpower can be developed like a muscle. 

In short, free will is a spectrum, and one’s position on the spectrum is largely determined by the absence of external control by others, the ability to judge wisely based on knowledge and logic, and one’s ability to exercise self-control. All of these factors are changeable through education and the practice of self-restraint.

author: @During_o7
text:
As a former determinist, the argument is quite compelling. However, it is actually deeply flawed. 

The problem with determinism is that the entire argument rests upon the assumption that everything physical is predictable, and because of that “fact”, we could predict all of your behavior. There are a lot of issues with this. 

1) We have no reason to believe that everything physical is predictable (quantum mechanics and complex systems)

2) The only proof that could be provided to prove a thing is completely predictable is to predict that thing with 100% accuracy. 

3) The only scenario in which a determinist would claim to be able to predict human behavior (with 100% accuracy) is one in which they have complete information on all matter and forces in existence (Omnipotence)

In other words, the axioms of determinism are fundamentally unprovable, given the conditions needed to prove it are impossible to obtain. 

You may also ask the determinist: “What can I do to prove to you that I have Free Will?” and their answer will logically be: “Nothing, because I could have predicted it”

So not only is their argument impossible to prove by their own admission, it is also unfalsifiable. 

Some determinists often respond that we cannot disprove Free Will because it does not exist, therefore we cannot disprove a negative. 

The issue with this is that you are not actually making a claim that Free Will does not exist. Rather, you are making the claim that because all physical matter is predictable, Free Will logically cannot exist. Claiming that all physical matter is predictable is by definition an empirical claim, meaning that determinists have the burden of proof to validate this claim, and, by proxy, “disprove” Free Will.

author: @davidclifford5124
text:
Whenever I listen to young philosophers, I’m always reminded of a book I once read by David Benatar called ‘Better never to have been’. I was astonished that someone in their right mind would want to argue that life is never worth living. I can certainly understand why some people reach a point in their lives, often tragically early on, when they decide that they have had enough and want to call it a day. But, for me, the idea that the experience of being alive is in some way intrinsically bad is incomprehensible. 

Needless to say, I was keen to get his book and consider his arguments which I thought would at least be interesting. Sadly, I wasted my money because his explanation was nothing short of nonsense. In particular, his arguments centred around an absurdly simplified view of what life actually is. Are all philosophers as foolish as he is, I asked myself. Thankfully, they aren’t. But I regularly come across so called philosophers that are close runners up and one is, in my view, Professor Robert Sapolsky. 

Now, my understanding of determinism is that, at the time when the planets were forming around our Sun four billion years ago, it was completely inevitable that I would be sitting here typing this comment. This is because the behaviour of every atom in the universe is subject to strict laws and that there is only one outcome at each successive second as to their relative positions and so on. Indeed, it is also the case that, although there is an uncertainty regarding the properties of sub-atomic particles as to their precise position and spin, this uncertainty evaporates as their combined positions are averaged out. In any event, it is something like that which doesn’t really interest me anyway. As a consequence, it could perhaps be possible for an experienced physicist to convince me that the universe was completely deterministic until the emergence of life. It is plausible, I suppose, that inorganic matter would have behaved strictly in accordance with fixed laws at all times. 

However, the emergence of life brought about an explosion in a level of complexity that would challenge the capacity of physical laws to completely control not just every atom but every cell that goes to make up the biological world in which we live. Four billion years later, many living creatures on Earth have evolved brains that have trillions of synapses, billions of neurons and countless electrical charges between them which, in the case of human beings, has enabled us to conceptualise situations that we experience, to identify possible alternative responses, to consider the possible outcomes of pursuing those various responses and evaluate the impact that those responses might have upon our fellow human beings. This capacity, like consciousness itself, has evolved over billions of years in response to the development of ‘competences’ as described in Daniel Dennet’s book, ‘From bacteria to Bach and Back’. ‘Thinking’ is not merely a physical or mechanical process subject to physical laws. Thoughts are, of course, ‘carried’ by electrical charges, as I understand it, across synapses but the information contained within the thoughts themselves are not controlled by ‘physical’ laws.

Free will, in my view, is the innate capacity of most healthy human beings and, indeed, possibly some animals, to consider various available options for action and to make a judgement about what particular option to select. That selection is not, in my view, contingent upon physical laws and in this way, we are responsible, under normal circumstances for the choices that we make. Of course, there are plenty of influences on our decision-making that originate, as Sapolsky says, from our genetic endowment, our experiences in the womb and early childhood, the culture in which we grew up and the society in which we live and so on. However, they are ‘influential’. They do not determine our choices. We are capable of making choices based upon our own intellect.

In any event, the argument against determinism has been put much more succinctly than I ever could and much more authoritatively by other experienced scientists and philosophers.

Your content is insightful and thought-provoking! Thank you. I truly appreciate the exploration of degrees of freedom and the idea of freedom existing on a spectrum. It seems to portray this "will" as something exceptionally special, untainted by causal factors (though admittedly influenced and determined by them), and essentially just "us." However, despite the subjective feeling of such uniqueness, objectively, this doesn't seem to be the case. The idea of a "will" representing the true "us," making choices without external factors, appears contradictory. Every choice we make is intricately connected to the causal matrix in which we are embedded. Our "will" is essentially born from this causal web, and our degrees of freedom are causally determined.

The proposition that our wills are shaped by both internal and external causes, and that our degrees of freedom are not entirely within our control, while simultaneously suggesting that we are free when engaging our causally determined will that is not independent of external factors, seems perplexing. It challenges my understanding, and the idea of our freedom being constrained by causality makes my brain hurt, lol..

author: @ark-L
text:
This is a great video! You almost made compatibilism sound coherent ;P

To be less snaky about it: I think the point about different gradations of freedom is useful for evaluating how we expect a given person to act, and thus how much of a danger they are to society, say, but I don't think it ultimately allows for the kind of "free" will that would allow us to maintain our colloquial—much less *legal*—use of the term. 

If someone murdered their lover in a jealous rage and regretted it immensely after, that's certainly much different than someone who murders their lover with glee and vows to do it to another. And as a society, we want for very good reason to treat them very differently. But are either of these individuals really more free than the other? Sure, the former was overtaken by the force of an acute passion in the moment, but is not the other being acted on by a kind of chronic passion at all times? If someone feels the urge to kill but resists it, if that act of resistance is also determined by all prior antecedent states of reality, then how can we really blame or praise someone for whether this "resist" action happened to come up for them as the last link in a chain of causes that started with the beginning of time? Compatibilism sometimes strikes me as looking at a long sequence of dominoes and circling, like, a section near the end where it wasn't obvious how the dominoes would fall and then saying about the last domino: "See! I couldn't tell exactly which domino was gonna hit it, so it must have had a choice! 

In other words, are we not, at any moment "m", doing what moment "m-1" led us to do? Obviously, this is in large part a restatement of determinism, so a compatibilist is theoretically committed to saying this state of affairs does not undermine their position, but I've still never heard a good reason (and I've suffered, btw, all the best attempts to try) why that's the case beyond playing semantics with the "free" part of free will (looking at you, Danny D). 

And appeals to the sense of control we *feel* when we take actions really doesn't amount to anything. Optical illusions work because we *feel* like we're seeing something which doesn't turn out to be there. Not to mention, that even the notion that we have a kind of homuncular, unitary self that could be the locus of this free will was more-or-less DESTROYED by the Buddha millennia ago—and modern science has only grown in support of this position. If the "self" is a story we tell our "selves", then how are the parts of that story that involve us actually being in control *not* part of this self-ifying narrative? 

Now, as a bit of a curveball, I'm a metaphysical idealist, so I think consciousness is the fundamental substrate of existence and the egoic "I" is really a pale inflection of the true "I" which is actually all there is and ever could be... but that still doesn't in any way allow space for free will of the kind that would justify most of the ways we use it! (I think Strawson's so-called "Basic Argument" does the best job of laying out a metaphysically-neutral denial of free will) To circle back, this is especially true of the legal system, at least in the US. If one really takes on the implications of the free will denier's position, then retributive punishment should obviously serve 0 percent of the function of law and yet, It's one of its major pillars. 

Sorry this is so long, and again, good work! But when it comes to compatibilism, just say *no*... not that you actually have a choice either way ;)

author: @ivankaramasov
text:
Free will understood as acting without external coercion is both coherent and normatively important. When an agent’s choices stem from their own reasons, dispositions, and evaluative commitments, rather than from threats or manipulation, we can meaningfully speak of autonomy and responsibility. This notion requires no metaphysical extravagance; it is simply the capacity to act in accordance with one’s psychological architecture.

The alternative conception, that an agent could, under perfectly identical conditions, have chosen otherwise, is logically untenable. If we imagine a complete rewind of the world, down to the agent’s memories, neurophysiology, motivational states, environmental cues, and microphysical configuration, then any divergence in choice would lack a causal basis. Either the agent chooses the same, or the difference is produced by indeterminacy. But indeterminacy is not agency; it is randomness. A choice that changes solely because a non‑rational, non‑motivational fluctuation occurred is not “free” in any meaningful sense. It is merely stochastic variation.

Thus, the only defensible notion of free will is the modest one: freedom from coercion, and the ability to act from one’s own reasons. The stronger counterfactual notion collapses into either incoherence or randomness, and neither supports the concept of responsible agency.

Who Is Actually Choosing? The Physics That Breaks Free Will

Two centuries ago, Laplace proposed a thought experiment (Laplace's Demon,1814) that still haunts physics: an intellect that knows the exact state of every particle in the universe, for whom the future would already be fixed. If we trace that idea forward through modern debates on determinism and quantum randomness into the Free Will Theorem from mathematicians John Conway and Simon Kochen, and finally into the neuroscience of Benjamin Libet's landmark experiments on conscious decision-making, we get no easy answers.

What I find most interesting isn't any single result but how the question keeps changing shape. The Free Will Theorem doesn't ask whether physics leaves room for free will . It asks what happens if you simply grant humans a minimal freedom to choose and follows the mathematics wherever it leads. Libet's work doesn't settle whether free will exists rather it forces a harder question about what "deciding" actually is at the neural level.

Are you writing our story or reading one that's already written?

author: @TerrythePhysicist
text:
What Sean Carroll ignores is the fundamental mind-body problem, which is a deeply open question.  I think the biophysically correct discussion of conscious and unconscious mentation must precede any coercive discussion of the free will on an organism by organism level.  To me the mind "rides" on top of a biophysical engine that produces consciousness and is obviously a necessary condition for it.  Now, the mind and its phenomenology are BOTH predictable and unpredictable at the same time.  Because as you drill down on how much "precision" is strictly predictable there is a transition at some level of detail as to when mental states and choices start to operate within the fundamental (and fully chaotic) fluctuations of the biomechanical system.  The quantum mechanics afoot in biophysics, like all other examples, DOES NOT PRETEND to predict individual outcomes, but rather expectation (average) values of observables given the imposed boundary conditions.  Moreover those averages are "fuzzed out" at various levels of uncertainty by clearly defined operators that define a fluctuation of any observable from its expectation value.

So if consciousness inventories its preferences and values to arrive at a decision, there is every reason to imagine that, at the lowest level, the outcome is highly determined by fundamental drives, viz. almost none will choose to suicide based on the color of the shirt chosen.  In contrast, it is probably quite random whether the shirt color will definitively predict the outcome of any romantic strategy one has in mind at the closet in the morning.

Similarly for games of skill like chess or billiards, while it is clear that a winner is determined by the sequence of moves chosen, it is not at all obvious that the mental "initial condition" when the game begins can predict which contestant will win.  At some level sufficiently delicate sequences of choices will always "feel free" to the mind executing them and it seems that the determinist's burden of proof is show that apparent freedom to be illusory.

author: @marvinedwards737
text:
There is a very good reason why people object to the notion that they "could not have done otherwise”. It’s called “cognitive dissonance”.

Suppose, you tell your child “I have two ice cream cones, chocolate and vanilla. You can choose either one, and I will have the other.” Then the child chooses the chocolate. Now, if you say to the child, “You could not have chosen the vanilla”, and your child is bright, she will say, “Either you were lying at first, or you are lying now. You told me I could choose the vanilla. Now you are saying I could not have chosen it! One of those must be false, because they directly contradict each other.”

And the child is correct, of course.

You’ve made a small error in your logic. You’ve equated what “can” happen with what “will” happen. You’ve assumed that if something “would not happen", then it “could not have happened”.

To eliminate the dissonance, try replacing “could not” with “would not”. If you say to your child “You would not have chosen the vanilla”, she will accept that. She knows that she prefers chocolate, and that given the same options, she would always choose chocolate. So, “you would not have chosen vanilla” does not produce any cognitive dissonance.

But she will not accept the notion that she “could not” have chosen the vanilla, because, after all, you just finished telling her that she could choose the vanilla, just before she chose the chocolate.

And this is always true whenever choosing shows up in a causal chain. In order to make a choice, we must first believe that we actually have two things that we can choose between. From the two things we “can” choose, we select the single thing that we “will” choose.

Thus, at the end of any choosing event, we will have the single thing that we “would” choose, and at least one other thing that we “could have” chosen, but didn’t.

The logical blunder has unfortunately become ingrained in the common definition of determinism, as implying that we “could not have done otherwise”, when all that is truly implied is that we “would not have done otherwise”.

When we say that we “could have chosen vanilla” we are implying that (a) we did not choose it and (b) that we only would have chosen it if circumstances were different. And this comports with the facts of the matter.

She could have chosen vanilla, but she would not have chosen it. This statement is TRUE in both its parts.

author: @Salv-lj8kj
text:
The question of consciousness, free will and cognition is one of metaphysics. Metaphysics is the study of the ultimate reality. Metaphysics entails ontology; the study of what categories of "things" exist. There are three broad ontological categories of things that exist: 1) Objective things - These are the physical things including all fundamental forces in the standard model (plus gravity), all the "particles" in the standard model and all their aggregations such as atoms, molecules, living cells, animals and plants. 2) Subjective things - These are the things of the Mind which include consciousness (awareness and self-awareness and free will) and the contents of consciousness (perceptions, thoughts, mental images, beliefs, emotions, etc.). 3) Abstract objects - Universal things; this is the Platonic realm.

The question is which ontological category of things is fundamental and which is/are derivative. If you believe that the Objective (physical) things are the ultimate reality, i.e. are fundamental and that the subjective things of the Mind are derivative, you are a Materialist. As Sean Carroll said, Materialism is the prevailing view in science, at least among academic scientists. If you believe that subjective things of the Mind are fundamental and that the physical things are derived from Mind, then you are an Idealist. One or the other...either Materialism or Idealism is true. I do not think there is any "excluded middle." For Materialism to be correct, it has to be the case that the electromagnetic force (which is the only fundamental force that comes into play in the physical brain) and its effects on the molecular components of the brain have to account for all of the phenomena of the subjective conscious experience of Mind listed above. That is a very tall order. Sean Carroll's answer to that question "emergence" is hopeless inadequate. Materialist scientists should be embarrassed by Carroll's very simplistic response. He is simply applying a label to a collection of intractable mysteries. Essentially what Carroll is saying is that somehow, all these capabilities of that which we call our conscious Minds listed above, just magically appear. Does that really sound like a scientific explanation?

So, which is correct, Idealism or Materialism? Stated another way, is Mind fundamental and physical things derivative? Or are Material things fundamental and Mind derivative? Well first off, one hint is that in our human experience we experience physical things only through our subjective conscious Mind. In other words, in our own experience Mind is fundamental and the objective physical things are derivative. Secondly, if we go back to Einstein's famous quotation: "The most incomprehensible thing about our universe is that it is comprehensible," from the standpoint of a Materialists, yeah, the observation that the universe eventuated in its own understanding would be astonishing and extremely improbable. However, from an Idealist perspective, that the universe eventuated in its own comprehension is exactly what you would expect. In other words, if our minds are instantiations of the ultimate Mind we would expect that we have free will and that Aristotle's Final Causes (teleology) would be apparent. And in fact, as Einstein's remark evidences, final causes are very apparent. Here is another way of thinking about it. What would be the signature of true libertarian free will? Well, the ability to direct our thoughts in order to discover new things and invent new things would be the signature of true libertarian free will. And I offer the sum total of all knowledge and all human artifacts and all human artistic renderings as a demonstration of that. These capabilities could not be explained by the putative programmatic free will functions proposed by Carroll's pseudo free will offered by compatibilism.

So only one objection remains: How is it possible for an immaterial infinite Mind to become embodied in a physical entity such that it can control the physical entity. Some philosophers such as Daniel Dennett feel that this is an insurmountable hurdle. Is it? No. Obviously, if Idealism is positing an ultimate entity that created the universe and all laws in it, clearly, there must be an interface between the two ontological categories. And the method of control would almost certainly involve quantum mechanics. Robert Russell, Henry Stapp, Richard Muller, Sir John Eccles are just some of the scientists who have shown that quantum mechanics allows for a conscious immaterial mind to control a physical entity. Richard Muller in his book Now, The Physics of Time says: "There is nothing in modern science that precludes free will."

I see some problems here.

If the premise is that "everything in the world is always governed by physical laws", obviously the will/brain/consciuosness of the subject will be too.
But this is a classic circular - and thus, useless - reasoning, since the conclusions are already implied in the premises (the subject and its will/brain/consciuosness are obviously part of the world). 

So we should analyze the premise.
How and why can we say that everything in the world is always governed by physical laws?
Certainly not thanks to Science.
Science has never answered (nor has it ever set out to answer) the question: "does it correspond to the truth that everything in the world is always governed by physical laws? And if so, how/why,?
Science is concerned with organizing and formalizing the physical laws themselves, not with the explanation of their existence, or their universality or whether or not they are present and absolute in every aspect of reality.

So... how and why can we say that everything in the world is always governed by physical laws ? Maybe because we have some empirical, direct experience of it? Yes, we have some degree of experience and intuition of it. But far from absoluteness and inevitability.
To start from the empirical experience/intuition of some level of  causality and for that reason LOGICALLY concluding that everything the world is always and inevitably governed by physical laws, at the highest conceivable degree.... is a fallacious ontological leap of faith.
It is the same mistake as observing a certain order, a certain intelligent (or intelligible) design in the world, and for that reason logically concluding for the ontological existence of the highest conceivable level of order and intelligent design (The Architect - GOD).

The fuzzy notion of "free will" persists largely because of sentimentality.  It makes no logical or scientific sense.  If the outcome of a decision is purely mechanical and predictable in advance, at least in principle, given enough information, then most people agree that the process is not "free".  However, the alternative is an outcome based on random, unpredictable, literally causeless factors.  It is not clear if such phenomena as *literally* causeless events exist, in contrast to events that have causes which are mechanistic but are too complex and difficult in practice to do the necessary measurements, collect the necessary information, and perform the complex computations.   However, in either scenario, it reduces to macroscopic phenomena that are either mechanistic or capriciously random.  Neither scenario could be called "free".  You would be talking maybe about magic, or angels, or something vaguely religious, but nothing that makes rational or scientific sense.  

The "free will" question was really settled a long time ago ("No"), but the annoying debate will persistent indefinitely.

author: @simongross3122
text:
Sorry.  This is, as you put it, a bit "loosey goosey"  You speak as though it is already known that the "laws of physics" are deterministic.  The very phrase "laws of physics" is misleading.  They are not laws.  They are models.  They are simply a shorthand way of saying that we have always observed something to proceed in a particular way.  That these initial conditions have always resulted in that outcome.  We invent the laws so that we can make very good but imperfect mathematical models.  Because the laws are thus invented (not discovered), there is no way to prove that the underlying laws of physics (if they exist) are deterministic.  You can make a model, but you can't prove that it is complete.  All you can do is take observations and measure their divergence from the model.

In fact, apart from observational and measurement error, these "laws" do not always precisely predict.  Even in classical physics there are problems like the "three body problem" which defies our ability to predict the motion of 3 bodies accurately.

So, what if the real world is not completely deterministic?  This would mean that the underlying "laws" cannot be deterministic either, but at best would be statistical with our current mathematics.  I don't want to invoke the quantum, but I'm sure you get my point.  What if the laws are only completely precise within rigidly defined boundaries of uncertainty and doubt?  (To misquote Douglas Adams).

I think that it is completely possible for there to be an underlying reality that defies analysis through our mathematics and models, precisely because we insist on determinism.  I think it is completely possible for there to be free will as part of that structure.  Not saying that there is, but I think it is possible.  So far, there is no proof, but Occam's Razor is probably on my side here.

I'm not sure that I agree with your take on "emergence" either.  That approach simply means that from simple building blocks we can get unexpected complexity.  While this is obviously true, it is not obvious that we have all the building blocks.  We have steadfastly avoided trying to find a free-will building block.

Not trying to be mystical, magical, religious or any other kind of woo-woo here.  Just pointing out that we do not know the full picture, and so far have not developed the tools to look for it.

To me, the real question is: What sort of physical structure needs to exist to be able to exercise free will?  What are the minimum requirements?

text: I dont think we CAN know if we have free-will or not at this point of time and maybe not ever. For instance, even if we do have "free-will", that "free-will" is still guided by evolution. From the big picture perspective, evolution seems to be guiding life in a negentropic fashion. However, we don't know what the end goal is or why there is even a force of evolution in the first place. From a more personal/little picture perspective of evolution guiding us, everything we "do" is determined by what we think will maximize positivity (negentropic growth) and/or minimize negativity (entropy). When we synthesize the big and little pictures, we see that even if we make mistakes in the little picture (i.e we "do" something that is not conducive to maximizing positivity/negentropic growth as a result of ignorance), we still can't help but learn and grow from our mistakes. This means that ultimately from the bigger picture perspective, we are still headed towards evolutions "goal" even if we make mistakes in our little picture day-to-day lives. So in conclusion, from both the little and big picture perspective, our "free-will" is really determined by evolution. It would therefore appear as though we don't have free-will by virtue of not knowing why we really do anything. However, it could very well be that upon reaching evolutions endgoal or perhaps somewhere along the journey, it might be revealed to us that we actually do have free-will by some means or another. Nonetheless, at this moment in time, all we can say is that it would appear as though we don't have free-will but simply can't say for sure. My guess is that if we ever can know the truth to the free-will question, it will at the very least require us to overcome the human condition 🤙

The human mind is very similarto artificial intelligence systems. These systems calibrate their decision making abilities by learning from the past examples of which decisions are optimal or correct based on clues about the problem. Once these calibrations have been complete, it's hardly a matter of choice, it's rather about what seems the most desirable according to all criteria involved at that current moment. 

The human mind is not just similar to an AI system, it's a system of AI systems that feed their outputs to each other as new inputs upon which to perform calculations. For example, if I want to decide what to wear to an event, I first make a decision about what the dress code should be if it's not already obvious, then based on my decision I might decide if I want to dress up or dress down, then I might decide what colors based on my emotional state on that day or at that moment.

I see the so-called free will as merely outputs of decision-making algorithms. However, we as humans have the ability to re-calibrate or deicion-making processes through education, to help us understand what should be desirable or undesirable irrespective to what our nature finds desirable, which oftentimes can be harmful.

This means that any "criminal" that walks the earth are not "criminals" at all, but neither are there any "heroes" or "saints" so to speak who do what we like to call "righteous" actions deserving of praise.

Because one of them "feels" right in the moment. In hindsight it may seem that it wasn't "right" but how can I tell as I cannot predict all possible outcomes of any action I take? I am blindly taking actions at all times, therefore I have no real choice. Taking it even further to a basal level: what if someone were to come stab me to death, would I have any choice but to die? What if I as a completely defenceless baby were killed of during infancy, where's the choice there? I was completely at the mercy of caretakers. Thus all my life has been completely at the mercy of others. Thus there is literally no choice whatsover. You are who you are, and you do what you do, that's all.

author: @ApPersonaNonGrata
text:
Sigh.
I agree with most of what he is saying here. But not all of it.
By that, I mean:
He is factually wrong about Libertarian Free Will.

It doesn't matter how many things we don't yet know about physics. 

The only thing we can replace physics with is magic.

 Since when do physicists propose magic as a driver in anything that happens in our minds?

Libertarian Free Will proposes and depends upon:
 Being able to generate WILL (desire; intent) purposefully 
without any prior (antecedent) physics-driven phenomenon "determining" (causing; necessitating) us into that purpose.
 
The only time we do a thing where that action is not intentional 
is when an action is automatic.

Automatic actions aren't "freely willed".
But neither are intentional actions, because we can't freely choose what our intentions will be.

Whenever someone wants to do a thing, they have reasons. 
Those reasons are driven entirely by physics.
It doesn't matter that we don't know everything about physics. That's like not being able to see every mechanism in a massive Rube Goldberg machine. 
It doesn't matter if some of the moving parts in that machinery are hard, squishy, round, square, or rely on distant, subtle, and invisible forces of push and pull.
The only way to generate that machinery's output with a mechanism that isn't physics ... would be magic. aka "uncaused events".

We don't always know "why" we choose one thing over another.
Whenever we do know why, ... that means we recognize some of the prior necessitating causes of our decision. 
Fear is a physics-driven phenomenon.
So is hunger, thirst, hope, joy, expectation of pleasure, avoidance of pain, etc..

Whenever we don't know why we "chose" one specific thing over another ... that ALSO means we didn't get to "freely will" ourselves into the desire that prompted the choice we made.

If we had an invisible, flying time machine with a window, went forward 10 years into the future, hovered over a park, observed local activities,
we could observe macroscopic events unseen.
If we come back to our original time and place,  rest for a moment, and then return to the same time and picked a different spot to hover/observe from (so that we don't collide with our invisible self from the prior time-travel visit), ...
we would either see everything happen the same exact way all over again (providing that everything is determined)
or 
we would see things happening differently (proving that microscopic randomness is real, in an otherwise-deterministic universe). 
 
Randomness, if that truly exists, would not enable Libertarian Free Will; Because that's literally the opposite of purposed. So it would do nothing to break us free of the limits inherent to deterministic physics. 

We do what we want to; within the limits of what we're able.
But we do not get to freely choose what we will "want" to do.

author: @georgegrubbs2966
text:
Very nice, Sean, but I humbly disagree on a couple of points.  

(1) You could not have done differently, because you did what you did after considering the options at a point in universal time.  Your statement is hypothetical and cannot be tested.  .

(2) To understand "free will," we must understand what "you" and "me" are.  We are that which emerges from patterns of neural networks, both of which obey the laws of physics (the emergence and the neural networks).  Let's label that emergence, "X".  X must have the capability to modify the other neural networks in the physical system that make up a human being.  It is the conscious controller of the physical system (remember that X is an emergence from patterns of neural networks).  We also call this the "self" ("me").  

X has access to memories and other states of neural activity in the physical system (the person).  Thus, X has preferences and biases based on genetics and experiences that come from memories and the system state.  

X is also subject to influences in the immediate environment that may subconsciously determine a decision, thus the decision is not free.  For example, suppose X is making a choice between chocolate and vanilla ice cream.  Traditionally, X would choose vanilla since that is X's favorite (it produces good internal feelings of pleasure).  However, there is a sign in the ice cream shop showing someone having a chocolate ice cream and they are having a great time.  This scene triggers a reward system in the nucleus accumbens (it releases dopamine) such that X chooses chocolate without being aware of what caused the choice.  The choice was not free.  Given the same circumstances, X would again choose chocolate.

Is it something infinitely more complex than any of the above?

The thing about free will is that whether I actually have free will or not, I still have choices to make. I still have to decide whether or not to pay the electric bill. author: @PierceArner
text:
Having free will OR having the illusion of free will are functionally identical in every way except for how you view them existentially. Neither makes any difference to the mechanics of how we behave and how much we're ever able to know about it.

The sensitivity of certain systems due to deterministic chaos means that having perfect predictions is impossible, even though they are technically feasible if that information were obtainable — which it's not. So it's one of those questions where it's exposing that the interest in pondering about free will is really more interested in asking whether or not there is an existential purpose to the idea of free will.

To which, I'd refer to the previous point and say that it's the ONLY purpose, and whether or not you want to view it one way or the other won't fundamentally change you, and your existence will continue being exactly as it's always been regardless of that understanding.
