author: @SkeletonLeiutenant
text:
This is gonna get lost on I imagine 99% of the people in here because everyone here is likely either an optimally functioning human being or an armchair/Reddit philosopher but, hey, why not, life's absurd.

Also, I realised halfway through writing this, some of what I was talking about was actually existentialism.

So I was thinking about modern characters and media that may be absurdist and strangely came to the realisation that most characters in the manga/anime Jujutsu Kaisen can be seen as absurdism vs existentialism.

Quick rundown for those who haven't seen it: In the setting, humans produce something called cursed energy, this creates creatures called curses that feed off human flesh and suffering. Some humans developed the ability to mould and use their cursed energy to see and "exorcise" curses.

So most of the heroes/protagonists, my current list being: Yuji Itadori, Megumi Fushiguro,  Nobara Kugisaki, Kento Nanami, Maki Zenin, Yuta Okotsu, Aoi Todo, Yuki Tsukumo, Choso and even the great Satoru Gojo.
Each of these characters see the absurdism of life and defy it by giving themselves a meaning that is ultimately saving people by killing curses: whether it be solely for the reason of saving people, to cure boredom, out of a sense of guilt, or even to overthrow a corrupt system within the secret society.
Even Gojo, who is a Messiah figure, one of the strongest beings of all time, leads an Existentialist life.

Whereas the many of series villains are that evil interpretation of absurdism which I'm now learning may be hedonism. Notably: Ryomen Sukuna, Mahito, Kenjaku, Haruta Shigemo, Juzo Kumiya, Jiro Awasaka.
They see the absurdity of life and say "Let it all burn".
•Haruta Shigemo, Juzo Kumiya and Jiro Awasaka are serial killers that kill because they enjoy it and don't want to be prosecuted for that, and they sometimes get paid for it. They took Absurdism and turned it into hedonism.
•Mahito is a curse born of human hatred, his powers let him shape and mould the soul/body of humans, so beleives he should be able to do whatever he wants. More of a hedonist as well.
•Sukuna was one of the strongest curse users of all time so he just does what he wants. He wants a world where he can do what he wants and he's strong enough to get that by brute force. He saw the absurdity and took to hedonism because he was the only man who truly could.
•Kenjaku is a curse user with an ability that gives him immortality if he can transfer his brain to a new body, he sees the absurdism in life, and so dedicates 1000 years of his unnaturally long life to enact a plan just to see how far he can push the physics of cursed energy.

There are exceptions to this as well:
•Hiromi Higuruma is a lawyer who sees the pointlessness of the justice system if the powerful can just rig it and when he reaches his breaking point, his acceptance of the absurd, he awakens his powers. He kills people he believes are corrupt or evil using his strongly decisive power based on the legal system and personal guilt, yet spares the main character Yuji when he claims he's guilty for the hundreds of thousands of lives taken by his hands when Sukuna possessed his body.
•Fumihiko Takaba: His powers allow him to do almost anything as long as he finds it funny and he takes nothing seriously... enough said... 

The most powerful thing I think is Yuji's speech to Mahito.
For context: Mahito has killed a lot of Yuji's friends and innocent people and Sukuna killed thousands using Yuji's body. All the while Mahito has been saying Yuji and he are the same.
Yuji says to Mahito after beating him in their final fight:
"I'll accept it, Mahito. I am you. I wanted to reject you. I wanted to pretend I didn't understand anything you said. But that's different now. I'll just kill you. And if you're ever reborn again as a new curse, I'll kill you then, too. You can change your name, change your appearance, but I'll still kill you again and again. I don't need meaning or a reason for it anymore. Maybe they'll be some meaning to be found from my actions several centuries after I'm long dead. But I'm sure I'm just... one big cog in the wheel. And I'll keep killing curses until I rust away.
Because that is my role in this war."

I believe that is Yuji accepting the absurd just like Mahito has, yet rejecting him and his ideals of true meaninglessness. He accepts there truly is no meaning and no reason to give yourself a meaning, yet chooses to anyway, spitting in the face of the immoral.

text: It's kind of funny that he imagined Sisyphus happy when Sisyphus literally has a task assigned by the gods. Kind of the opposite of Absurdism imo. Or at least a poor example. Like, his task is to struggle and achieve nothing yet it's still an externally given task. Also, I don't think a moral framework is necessary for a life outlook like this. If anything Absurdism lends itself to moral anti-realism than any prescriptive system. I feel like in trying to assign musts the best part of living in a meaningless world is lost, that there is no must, no meaning, you're free to shape it all however you like. It's fantastic. Anything from the most menial to the grandest ambition can be given as much or little meaning as you want. You get to personally craft what importance and meaning is. That was a power at one point only thought gods capable of yet if you recognize cosmic meaninglessness, absurdity, you get the power to make a fully legitimate meaning for yourself that coexists with everyone else. It's like living in a world of your own creation, but everyone else also gets to do it and can collaboratively make it richer for everyone else without having the ability to make it worse. At least that's my view of things. Instead of needing to resist meaninglessness while simultaneously recognizing it as a rebel you simply see the beauty in it as it is and appreciate that emptiness as it means you get to fill that void with whatever you want and can change it at anytime.

text: I think interpreting Camus’ line of thought is actually pretty simple. In his early works, he realizes that life is meaningless which leads him to believe that one should act whichever way will bring them the most happiness in life until life is over. He later comes to understand that life being having no overarching meaning, doesn’t make life completely meaningless, as the meaning becomes finding as much of that happiness as possible. The issue he was posed with is that one who finds the most possible happiness in life will impede on the happiness of many other people in their life. So now the purpose of life is to find the balance of finding your own happiness without taking away from other’s opportunities to do the same.

It also seems almost impossible to "meaninglessly create" on the extra-cognitive level. If you enter a flow state during creation, then felt meaning is natural. And I wonder whether this comes from a hidden assumption that if a phenomenon can be explained by its conditions, it is therefore less real than its constituents.

author: @PavlosBlachopoulos
text:
Hello! Thank you for bringing up the point at 20:49, I believe it is an extremely interesting and somewhat overlooked aspect of the Myth. It's something I also struggled with for a long time.

Camus gives a clearer answer in "The Rebel", where he ties ethics to the recognition of other people also existing in the absurd condition. By recognizing others as absurd people (or rebels, in the case of this work), we start creating some sort of code of ethics. The interesting part is how this "code" is created. Camus seems to adopt the "negative" position. So rather than "doing unto others as we would like to have done to us", we "do not do to others what we would not like to have done to us". The Rebel creates clear boundaries, and they are boundaries that are not to be crossed by others, or by the Rebel themselves.

As for the possible answer he provides in the myth, I believe it would be something like the following: The absurd man is not at best amoral, or possibly even evil. The absurd man does not recognize value judgements in such a way. He acknowledges morality, he just does not give the consequences of morality the same weight that an existentialist might. He considers decisions and implications calmly, and does not declare a person guilty or not guilty, but responsible or not responsible.

In other words, Camus seems to adopt some form of consequentialism - we do not seem to care about the intent so much, rather if someone is responsible or not for something. This has its own set of problems, but it's how I interpret ethics in the Myth.

Again, thank you for bringing this up!

Faust is the archetype of the absurd man. He can live eternally as long as he never gets satisfied, or "happy". Once he does, Mephistopheles wins and takes his soul. But as long as he stays unfulfilled and his goals in a way thwarted, he is ok. He's got all the features, even his rebellion against God that is silent.

As to the freedom, I don't think it's a real problem, at least not in the case of murder. If he comes to the conclusion that you should not stop living out of rebellion, then there is no reason one would accept murder, so life itself is meaning to the absurd man. He probably could have gone further and talked about family and those other things. In a way, Faust gets some of that meaning through the community. It would make sense that those things would be seen as life and valued as such even indirectly. It's also why Sisiphus is happy, since he is alive and still in rebellion.

I think there is a parallel to make with the book of Job. In the book, everybody wants Job to curse God and die. That's the normal thing you are supposed to do when you loose everything. But that is giving up in a way, because Job is innocent, so he is right in rebelling against this and God and his act of rebellion is actually to stay alive. Now of course in that case, he gets his stuff back with interest, so there is hope, so it's the difference with the absurd man. There is no hope and God does not reply and is not there to fix the injustice if you persevere. What you see is what you get. All that is left is to reject that silence, rebel against it. So I don't really see your problems with it insofar as morality goes, or why it would not be satisfying. Either you seek another goal and then you live in that illusion, or you rebel against that lack of illusion and come back to something probably better in the end, but more free of the extras. author: @Nivexity
text:
Egoism is the only philosophy that is purely descriptive, never stepping over the is-ought line, and its foundational premise would be that we're not blank slates, nor born without values. Instead, you're born with values which are provided to you through evolution, you're satiated when you eat, comforted by warmth, excited when aroused, etc. These values exist strictly as part of your experience, you'll mediate toward and away from them at your desire. As there are an infinite number of potential ways your values can be experienced, your freedom to choose how you wish to experience, including its extinguishment, is an egoist's highest value. Ultimately, this is merely a description of a human's nature. However, because such values are easily usurped by sacrosanctity, the authentic egoist is one who actively rejects the reification of values (to make sacred).

Absurdist conclusions are flawed; they reify an existence beyond your own perspective, the "world," which is your model of reality and the source of your values, ends when you die. Maybe your experience is not worth living if it doesn't yield any potential for increasing one's experience. For Sisyphus, the process of effort isn't without thought, for as long as Sisyphus can expand on perspective and refine capabilities, the eternal effort is not without value. Sisyphus may find pleasure in the relief of walking down the mountain, and may come to find it worth the effort entirely. However, this hypothetical doesn't map onto our perspective, as we presume all things end, and the continuous torture of pushing a boulder only ever makes sense as temporary to us.

Regarding the concerns of morality, it already doesn't really exist in the way people think, as morality is the relationship between values and action. However, if value is derived from experience and you can only experience your perspective, such that all other perspectives are formulations from your own, then morality is not only subjective but entirely in accordance with your own will. The truth might sting a little, but the only way a society can move forward is if we accept that everyone has their own values they wish to maximize, pushing for greater liberty while filtering what is currently incompatible will be in each authentic egoist's interest. By each I mean, if your egoist goal is to increase your experience and overall capabilities, and you can't rule the world, then you're left to participate in such way whereby your own liberty is guaranteed. For a society, that would necessarily be advocating for greater liberty to the citizenry, not because you hold an altruistic goal, but because it serves your own interest to do so, a great altruist is an egoist.

To an egoist, a serial killer is not "evil," they're incompatible, and one who explores murder in full dive vr would be compatible as the action does not lead to anti-liberty. As society grows, as do our ability to encompass more values, and as such, increase our overall liberty, which in return increases what we'd perceive as well-being. To me, well-being is best described as the opposite of death, where death is the absolute loss of choice and experience, well-being is as much choice and experience as you're willing to desire.

About 25 minutes in, and it seems, to me at least, that Camus was trying to identify the ways in which absurdism interacts with the social contract. As you said, Camus' absurdism treats all actions equally, but I don't remember you discussing the consequences of said actions. I'd argue that absurdism, and the knowledge thereof, acts as an impetus, a driving force that drives us to act. Why should we just sit around waiting when there are actions to be taken, futures to be discovered? If all possibilities are equally significant and insignificant, why not explore as many as possible? 

That is where the social contract comes in and restrains our actions through the threat of consequence. I could help my uncle jack off a horse, or I could help my uncle, Jack, off a horse. Both actions are equally insignificant, as no one would be bothered by either in the proposed situation. The former, however, has a much less desirable outcome when compared to the latter, as jacking off a horse is much less socially acceptable (potentially resulting in the ridicule of myself and my ego) while the latter is something seen as courtesy. As such, I believe the consequences of seemingly equivalent actions is where Camus had erred.

Just because we are free to act how we please, does not mean we are freed from the results of our actions. Hence, absurdism permits anything, but that does not mean nothing is forbidden.

At least, that is how I have chosen to interpret it.

But maybe that’s because the ultimate lesson there is the opposite of The Myth of Sisyphus, especially the part I liked least: the endless repetition.

It doesn’t mean it wasn’t once beautiful, that we didn’t put great care into it, or that it didn’t bring us peace and joy, or even wisdom. For a brief moment, it exists, and that existence is all that matters.

The fact that something doesn’t last should not matter at all. Nothing lasts. Everything that ever lives will die. The Earth will die, the Sun will die, and the universe will eventually turn dark.

The more aware we are of the impermanence of things, the more we should focus on the moment and also remind ourselves not to take anything for granted.

The denial of radical freedom has never made sense to me. Existentialism as a framework acknowledges the is and isn't of conditions and circumstances. You don't need absolute freedom to be free. Your status and organism, while coinciding with limits in cultural customs and physical capacities, do not determine your being. If you believe that you are a subject with a will, how can that not be free? How can a self-determining, sentient being be called "not free" because there exist obstacles and limits to the accomplishment of literally any conceivable desire. If anything, it is a testament to the imagination and creativity of the individual to conceive of freedoms they are not explicitly afforded.

author: @ethankillion786
text:
I think that Sarte's concept of absolute freedom is maybe a little problematic but not unsalveagable.

Sartre sets up authenticity as sort of the end goal, but authenticity is strictly internal. The material world is included in one's facticity, but you can be authentic regardless of facticity so long as you align transcendence and act in good faith.

To me, Sartre had lots of outs. He could have tied facticity to being-in-itself, transcendence to the realm of being-for-itself, and the ethics to being towards-others and then defined authenticity as aligning these three modes of being.

Sartre does seem to recognize the difference between freedom to choose/act and the actual agency/power to achieve results. A prisoner pn death row with hours to live and Elon Musk have equal ontological or theoretical freedom. But musk's choices almost all result in better outcomes.

Sartre also seemed to recognize that it was as a practical matter, impossible to achieve or maintain good faith. So he could have introduced a system of ethics whereby we can make it easier for others to be more authentic. He pretty much gets there in No Exit.

The problem with No Exit is that it still treats others as objects. They would all be better off and more authentic if they stopped being assholes. But it's still a selfish incentive. There is no like we should helping because we should feel bad for the hatred she suffered as a lesbian, or Garcin having at least tried to be noble but just understandably not being brave enough when faced with death. It's all very transactional where the strategy is to be nice to others only to the extent it helps you. But it's still a humanist play that at least shows why other people matter.

I think Beauvoir keeps Sartre's theoretical framework largely intact, with just a few modifications. Other existentialists differ more from Sartre but still manage to come up with philosophies that I view as both existentislist and humanist.

So yeah, anyway. I think that Sartre had competing takes on things that he could not reconcile but did not want to give up and then he just started getting into crazy convoluted concepts like the gaze or going off on a tangent into dialectical materialism and getting increasingly impenetrable.

But that's on Sartre. I don't think it's necessarily a problem with existentialism itself, or even Sartre's Being and Nothingness. As stated in the piece, there is nothing wrong with adjusting your philosophy. Sartre just kinda went off the deep end when he tried.

author: @FigureOnAStick
text:
I think that there is one aspect of the dialectic between freedom and constraint that deserves more attention. Freedom and constraint are paradoxically linked, and so cannot easily be divided into a good/bad binary.

To explain what I mean, consider what is required to master a skill, drawing, for example from a state of absolute ignorance. The first stage of learning is the first discovery of a potential capacity- that a pencil makes graphic marks, and that graphic marks can be used to produce an image. The second stage is the stage of creative play- the exploration of the relationship between your actions, the the results,they produce, and the way those reults feel- scribbling and doodling. After some time, one may find that the absolute freedom to make any mark is also a constraint, because they can't direct the outcome in any meaningful way. The third stage, deliberate practice, is the deliberate imposition of constraint in the form of disciple, which narrows ones options from a potentially  infinite of actions to a very narrow set of those that yield the results you want, in drawing, these are the skills of form, composition, perspective, value, etc. After that is another round of creative play, exploring the full potential of the skills won through deliberate practice. This cycle repeats back and forth, occasionally punctuated the the unexpected discovery of new degrees of freedom and constrained more broadly by wider context of need (ie, you can't just sit around and draw all day forever, you have to make a living for yourself more comprehensively).

Given the liberatory direction of philosophy as a project, it is understandable why freedom is usually held in higher regard than constant- philosophy is intended to free the thinker from the restraints of convention after all- but I think this is a misreading of the situation. After all, the billionaire tycoon is an extraordinary free individual, largely unconstrained by physical or social resistance, and billionaires also fucking such and make things harder for everyone else to support that freedom. Rather than attempt to assign absolute moral value freedom and constraint (freedom=good, constraint=bad), we should recognize them as moral qualities insofar as the dynamic relationship of freedom and constraint within a material system yields ethically charged outcomes, good or bad. We humans, as autonomous beings within the system, have the freedom to choose how to respond to our circumstances and shape the world, and we humans are also social animals living within a material ecosystem, constrained by the laws of physics and our biological  needs and the conventions of the communities on which we depend. It's a far more complex relationship with freedom and constraint than simple moral absolutes, but it's also more grounded and useful approach to the matter

After I converted to Catholicism, I went to college intending to become a philosopher. After a while they cut off my financial aid and I had to drop out. text: I have to disagree with the conclusion. It's not that existentialists weren't aware of the constraints that limit the individual's expression, they just didn't emphasize it. Kierkegaard's point is that while these 'quantitive determinations' change the demands on finding one's authenticity remains practically the same in all epochs. I fear that not focusing on the individual but on society creates this implicit notion that 'I know how I could find my authenticity but I am being suppressed' - this sort of Camusian idea that Sisyphus is happy through his hatred of the injustice of the world (Camus criticized existentialism btw). Alongside freedom, Kierkegaard also embraced the term 'resignation' which recognizes this problem but doesn't succumb to it - it invites the individual to seek authenticity in his/hers everyday life rather than to objectify himself/herself while waiting to be defined by some political or social Third party.

I get the objective/social angle, but the important over-arching bit is that the universe has no inherent meaning. As Sam Harris put it, It cares as much for us as it did the Dinosaurs and an asteroid could wipe us out sooner than we would like to think about.
It's human to wonder and ask about why there is something rather than nothing, but asking "why the universe" is just as silly a question as "why mount Everest".
A lot of the time "why" is not a relevant or useful question. Humans project agency onto too many things that we shouldn't. This is exactly how religions are created and upheld. 
Existentialism is not just a useful and more accurate life philosphy, but a tool against irrational, unreasonable, and/or unrealistic dogma and discourse.
The "burden" of making your own life as meaningful as you want, and understanding there is no after-life, means you cherish this life and your very limited time on this pale blue dot.

Quantum mechanics tells us that the basis of reality as we describe it is truly random, and chaos theory tells us that even with a perfect description of reality, it cannot be predicted in a world where measurement is imperfect, independent of quantum theory. So rationalism is only a success in the sense that we have rationally proven the limits to our ability to describe the world, so to explain existence, we need something else. author: @dialaskisel5929
text:
Our capacity for dread due to the  the apparent indifference of the universe is due to the development of our sapience.

Our sentience evolved into sapience to give us access to reason and to logic.

Our capacity for reason and logic was developed as a tool to help us adapt to our environment and perpetuate our lives - it is a tool for our survival.

This is the innate fallacy with negativistic philosophy - they attempt to separate themselves from bias by trying to solve their problems entirely a priori.  By putting reason, logic, and abstract theoretical concepts first.

However, we can find, due to the way life all the way down to the cellular level operates, that life inherently WANTS to continue living.

Using pure reason to negate the will-to-live forgets the fact that reason exists to serve the will-to-live, and allows life to overcome the obstacles to its continued existence.  

This isn't to say that one shouldn't use reason, it is vital and allows us to survive and thrive.  And, historically speaking, the more peoples embrace reason, the better they tend to adapt and increase their quality of life compared to those who do not.  But taking the innate positivity that is the will-to-live, love, beauty, and happiness out of the equation is pointless, logically flawed, and ultimately self-defeating.

I found that, after the realization, the way to life practically lies in complete immersion. I find it in making music with a friend, even just singing, or in listening to music that I can just describe as sounding like being filled with magic to my ears, or in sports, but also in dancing. The reason that meditation works so well for me is that it removes the layer of constant doubt and meaninglessness, which may be true, but inpractical to everyday life and me just wanting to have a good time. It's quite hard to enjoy enjoyable things and spending "a life well lived" when I carry my excessive thinking and questioning everywhere.
I think that Nihilism can really be a mental disease, since I experienced it myself and still feel the lingering dissonance every now and then in my thoughts. I think this is why the flow is mentioned so often nowadays: it makes us forget our existential dilemma, it makes life meaningful for a while (but if then, I think about life having meaning right now, I will lose the momentum and the flow).
If you read this up to here, I would be interested in what activity you like to get soaked into!

I still don't believe in objective morality, here's why.
Firstly I disagree with the principle of finality. I have a couple of questions regarding this principle. Does everything have exactly one final end or could some things have multiple purposes? Are there things that have no final ends? What is a final end of a rock? What makes a rock a good rock or a bad one? Also the example you used regarding trees is bad because oxygen is merely a byproduct of photosynthesis. The true purpose of photosynthesis is to produce sugar for plant's nutrition. Further more, the purpose of a tree is more complex, and more importantly, not objective at all, but relative. To a tree, it's own purpose is to sustain itself and reproduce, while to a human the purpose of a tree may be to provide oxygen, fruit or lumber. But what would be it's purpose to a fish, a star, or a rock? Lastly I would like to adress your reasoning for this principle to be true. First of all, calling it self-evident is a red herring. You claim that it requires no syllogism but than you proceed to prove it by reductio ad absurdum, which is a form of syllogism with premises being: "if the negation of a claim is false, than the claim is true" and "the opposite is false". The first problem is that you didn't negate your claim correctly. If your claim is that everithing has a certain purpose, than a negation of that would be that some things don't have a purpose. Instead you claim that the interlocutor must deny that anything has any purpose, which to me just seems like a strawman. This argument further false apart by introduction of a claim that the purpose of thinking is to get to truth and thus by dismissing it, the argument cannot be true. Firstly, the statement that thinking is only for seeking truth is rigid and incomplete. A writer might think about fiction, which is false, but you probably wouldn't call that bad thinking that didn't fulfill it's purpose. One might think about hypotheticals in order to plan ahead. This kind of thinking doesn't have anything to do with truth or falsehood. Secondly, the absence of purpose of thinking has nothing to do with truthfulness of interlocutor's argument. Things can happen even regardless of their supposed purpose. For example, a rock may be thrown even though it isn't it's inherent purpose. All in all, I think the principle of finality demonstrates a very narrow and rigid way of thinking that over-simplifies the nuanced natural mechanisms. To think that everything must have a purpose and happens for a certain purpose is naive and not at all objective, but rather entirely subjective.

author: @666PANDEMONIUM
text:
First of all, natural objects do not have "purposes." They have functions. For example, a tree can produce oxygen, that is one of its functions. However, producing oxygen is not the only thing that the tree can do and it is not the reason for the tree's existence. You are confusing your observation of what the tree can do with your idea of what the tree ought to do from your human-centric perspective. 

Second, even if I do grant you the premise that things exist for "purposes" how do you know what the purpose of all of these things are? If I claim that the purpose of a fruit is to spread seeds and you claim that the purpose of a fruit is to be eaten, how do we prove which of us is correct? Both of our claims are unfalsifiable, since there is no way for us to check what the objective purpose of a thing is without falling prey to our own biases. Can a single object have multiple purposes? If so, which purpose should it maximize when those purposes conflict with each other? 

Thirdly, this argument has failed to bridge the is/ought gap. For a moment, let's say that the purpose of human females is to have children. This does not explain why human females OUGHT to have children. Why ought things behave according to their purpose? What is that prescriptive idea grounded in? Why should the "natural order" be upheld? What if one wants to destroy the natural order? Why shouldn't they? If they have both the ability and will to act against the natural order what reason do they have to follow it?

The first problem, of course, as in almost all discussions of morality, is the lack of clarity about what is meant by ‘objective’, ‘subjective’, “relative” and ‘absolute’, which makes the whole thing rather unintelligible.
One contradicts oneself by saying that the existence of final causes is ‘obvious’ and ‘true in itself’ and then arguing by reductio ad absurdum... If one needs to argue, it does not seem like something that is obvious or true in itself. Next, I would readily admit that final causes exist in the sense of causes that enable something to continue to exist (thinking is made possible by the brain; it is in order to continue thinking that we have retained a brain), but not in the sense of causes that bring something into existence (it is in order to think that the brain came into being), and it is a mistake to equate final causes with ‘meaning’ or ‘purpose’.
Furthermore, it is highly doubtful that everything has a final cause. There is a great deal of contingency in nature.
Finally, the author of the video admits that a heart that functions poorly is not morally bad but says, without justification, that a man who eats poorly commits a moral evil. This shift, which a moral non-realist will refuse to make, is precisely what needs to be justified in order to prove an objective morality. We are missing the point.

The word "objective" has a specific definition, meaning detectible, measurable, or deducible via formal logic and invariant of the observer.

If natural law theory and intrinsic finality were objective, then there would not be serious disagreement between theologians. We all know there is considerable disagreement. To say otherwise is intellectually dishonest. Natural law theory and intrinsic finality are interpretive methods, i.e. *subjective*.

An example: Alice sees that humans are cooperative by nature and value life. She concludes by natural law that killing humans is immoral. Burt, however, has studied history and has observed that humans are greatly violent towards each other. In fact, the further back you go to where humans are less separated from nature, he notices that people kill each other even more. Killing appears to be a natural inclination of humans. Natural law theory would then say that killing is not immoral. The two observers have different perspectives; if natural law was objective, then there would not be a difference in perspective.

I say this as a regular churchgoer - don't make weak arguments. You lend no credibility to a Christian morality by doing so. A philosophy doesn't have to be objective to have moral truth.

Why gay sex might be brought up in a utilitarianism lecture:
There are a few common (and lazy) reasons:
	1.	“Harm Principle” debates — Utilitarianism, especially under thinkers like Mill, evaluates actions based on harm or pleasure. Some instructors use gay sex as an example to ask: “If it causes pleasure and no harm, can it be morally wrong under utilitarianism?”
	2.	Social taboos vs. moral wrongness — They try to contrast social discomfort with actual ethical reasoning, using sex-related topics to push that line.
	3.	Cultural relativity — A bad attempt at showing how moral judgments have shifted, often done in a clunky or borderline offensive way.

The problem:
These examples often:
	•	Derail into debates about personal identity instead of philosophical principle
	•	Are poorly framed, mixing social attitudes with ethical reasoning
	•	Don’t clarify anything about utilitarianism itself, which is about outcomes — not cultural taboos

What they should be doing:
If the point is to test utilitarian logic, use clean examples:
	•	Should you lie to save a life?

author: @lftr_react
text:
Singer's perspective on the issue of charity is out of focus. It assumes universal responsibility for every individual rather than the individual responsibility required by natural law (which is to say, the system in which we exist).
One could argue that, in order to survive in the system groups commonly need to work together. This is true, but it is not charity. In these cases you are working together in a shared interest for which you individually are involved. As you scale this up the direct effect of your involvement affects your personal situation at a diminishing rate. At a certain point, the system does not require your involvement with such things in order for you to thrive. When you reach that line, the responsibility shifts to those which are within the reach of the issue or hardship requiring attention. Even if you have a surplus of resources, you should likely not cross that line. The system actually requires those in the area of effect to attend to the issue or they may eternally be incapable of attending to it. This is a feature of the system. Do not feed the bears, as it were.
In the case of the shallow pond, you are in the area of effect. Additionally, the scenario goes beyond charity and enters into the arena of emergency. There is neither time nor capability for the child to resolve the issue and the cost of inaction is an ultimate price. Such a situation does not comport to that which may be categorized a matter of charity.

author: @Once_Upon_A_Time_in_Tartaria
text:
I've met Singer as well. Good dude, but I fail to be impressed with his conclusion. I think his examples are an excellent way to introduce the concept of moral philosophy. So many people, including singer himself, think that philosophical ethics or moral reasoning are simply a quest to find out and declare what constitutes the "right" morality. Maybe it's because of my own personal interest in the phenomenological School a philosophy, but I think that just misses the point. The more interesting thing is to look at how these hypothetical situations and various thought experiments reveal the moral calculus that our minds use in order to make decisions. Ethics, after all, is merely the study of the process by which we adjudicate competing value claims within our thought process. What I like about ethics is that it combines our reasoning AND our emotional experience, what Heidegger would define as Sorge, or that we experience the capacity to "care", that the things that occupy our intentionality MATTER to our sense of our well-being.

...kinda like what Hume is talking about with moral sentiments.

Mind you, I'm not saying that that such an approach is a slippery slope to emotional solipsism,or moral relativism. I just think the more appropriate question is, within the broader context of the totality of the experience of Dasein, it behooves us to understand HOW we arrive at our conclusions about the nature of virtue. Too often, these philosophers are far too eager to jump to PRESCRIPTIVE claims, rather than less grandiose, but more phenomenologically rigorous claims.

The better question is " why does it feel obvious that we don't feel the same way about donating to Oxfam as we do about getting our jacket dirty?"

author: @HelicopterRidesForCommunists
text:
No one can figure out what the problem is with Singer’s argument? Well, first of all what is a “luxury”? Buying coffee at a coffee shop is a luxury? Ok, so suppose people were to begin acting on Singer’s mortality and so instead of frequenting their favorite coffee shop they start sending it to a charity organization which (supposedly) “efficiently” transfers money towards famine relief. What would happen to that coffee shop? It would go bankrupt and close down. The employees? Would lose their jobs and their incomes. No one is spending money on their goods/services anymore. Now what happens to every other “luxury” people spend money on? There would be a chain-reaction within the economy and a self-induced recession would occur. Now think about this - where were the coffee shops getting their coffee beans from?  Perhaps it was from an area near the famine and it was one of the only sources of income for the locals. Now that the shops no longer exist to buy their beans their income dries up and they lose their farm or business.

So there are several problems with the argument. Its not as simple as dragging a drowning child out of water - that is a direct action that you know with a high degree of certainty will save the child which is why the vast majority would do it. Conversely it is not obvious that sending money to a charity organization will “efficiently” aid famine relief - just this morning before coming across this video I saw a video about a news story of a non-profit homeless organization and how they got millions of dollars of donations and grants and how they reported their expenses - over the course of several years the salaries they were paying ballooned and the amount spent on services and goods for the homeless became a minor percentage, and if that wasnt bad enough the organization was spending money on absurd things instead of focusing on things that are most essential and helpful for the homeless.

So there is a low degree of certainty that those suffering from famine would even benefit from it. 

Aside from that, this is actually a question of economics. If people began spending money as Singer proposes they do the economy would dramatically shift in a cascading affect and who knows how that would turn out? It could easily make the entire world’s population much much much worse off and almost definitely would as the single greatest factor for eliminating hunger/ famine/ starvation has been the introduction of market economics to developing areas.

text: I have been thinking about your video on famine, affluence and morality and think that I have an objection. I get the pond example, where jumping in to save the child is something we must do with a truly insignificant loss to us (the person who does the saving). But when he applies it to a way of life, one where you can never get coffee, or eat out, or ever buy nice and expensive clothes or a nice car is far fetched. Think of it like the utilitarians: when you add up all the things you have to give up, it is no longer insignificant. You would have to change your entire way of living, give up time cooking at home, and experiences of connecting with friends at restaurants, you would have to give up potentially a lot of seemingly insignificant things, but over time they add up. Picture it like this, if you were walking past the child in a puddle, and you saved him and got wet and muddy, that is fine because you go home and dry off and clean off the mud. But what if you lived in a world where that happened all day, all the time, all around you. You would never have time to dry off, you would always be muddy, and suddenly getting wet and muddy goes from a relatively insignificant thing to an entire lifestyle with constant loss that you must experience to keep saving the children. If you are a utilitarian martyr, it might make sense to keep saving the children, or giving up a coffee to save a life, but in the big picture it is NOT a insignificant loss that you take on, it is extremely significant. If you are a strict utilitarian, you will agree that this is still what you should do, because your life being far worse ends up saving thousands, which utilitarians think is worth it, but then again, the argument is as flimsy as strict utilitarianism.

02:29 - Utilitarianism: This ethical theory, introduced by Jeremy Bentham, states that actions should be based on producing the greatest overall balance of pleasure minus pain. It focuses on the consequences of actions and treats pleasure and pain as the ultimate moral factors.

06:35 - Thought Experiment: Robert Nozick's thought experiment involves an experience machine that can provide any desired experience. It challenges the idea that pleasure alone is the sole determinant of moral value, highlighting the importance of other aspects such as control, genuine experiences, and interpersonal relationships.

10:48 - Criticisms of Utilitarianism: H.J. McCloskey presents a counter-example to utilitarianism using a scenario where a sheriff must frame an innocent person to prevent a riot. This demonstrates a conflict between utilitarian calculations and commonly held moral intuitions, suggesting limitations to the theory.

18:26 - Kant's Moral Theory (Deontology): Immanuel Kant's deontological theory focuses on the intentions (maxims) behind actions rather than their consequences. The moral permissibility of an action is determined by whether its maxim can be universally accepted, irrespective of the outcome.

29:07 - Aristotle's Moral Theory (Eudaimonia): Aristotle argues that human beings have a unique purpose or function and that achieving eudaimonia (flourishing or fulfillment) is the ultimate goal. Eudaimonia is attained through the exercise of virtues and realizing one's potential as a rational being.

author: @Reddles37
text:
I tend to believe in utilitarianism, but an important point that a lot of counterarguments seem to miss is that you need to work through all the long-term consequences of your actions. So with the sheriff example, maybe framing the person could have good short-term effects, but upholding justice would be better for society and lead to less suffering in the long run. It's like saying I could get a lot of pleasure if I went out and blew all my savings on drugs, which is true but would make me unhappy later once I'm broke and an addict.

I think the main issue with consequentialism in general is that it's just too much work to think through all the effects of every action, and there is a lot of uncertainty involved. That's where the idea of deontological rules comes in, they give you a (relatively) simple system for making decisions in real life without having to stop and draw up a flow chart. But in principle the rules should be derivable from utilitarianism, based on what types of actions tend to on average produce the most benefit and least harm in the long term. It's essentially the same as the idea of type 1 and type 2 thinking, where we use simple heuristics to make snap judgements but then if necessary we can go back and think it through slowly and logically.

One question that kind of gets sidestepped is the distinction between "good" and "necessary." Utiilitarianism focuses on the utility necessity of an action and just calls that the moral choice. Because every action has a possible utility, that utility could supercede all other actions and become the most necessary, and therefore the most good.

For example, "frame an innocent man or all life in existence will be ended" DEFINITELY doesn't make framing the man "good," but i would argue it definitely makes it NECESSARY.

By contrast, the Kantian approach would say "nope, you have to let all life be extinguished. Sorry. Better luck in the next universe."

Both are wrong because they're conflating what you should do morally and what you should do practically.

author: @Flynbourne
text: I know that it is super easy to write off Kant’s philosophy as being rigid to the point of absurdity.  Because if we just take the first derivative of a statement ie “lying is wrong”, it is easy to find exceptions.  It is also possible to find conflicts with other  categorical imperatives.  Ie. lying is wrong.  And also “knowingly causing harm” is wrong.  But you can have many many situation where these categorical imperatives are in direct and insoluble conflict.   So unless Kant was a complete imbecile, surely the categorical imperative must give regard to context.  But that’s being very generous, because the term “category” typically encompasses actions in a range of situations.  The question becomes how specific are these categories.   Is it “all lying is wrong”, or is it “all lying except that which preserves human life is wrong”.   I think that Kant’s insight (which is never emphasised) is that he appeals to our sociological morals.

*The law application algorithm.*

We know the common punishable offences - murder, theft, assault, rape, hacking, incitement of violence, etc - these are punishable by current rules pretty much everywhere you'll go.
So, provided you don't do anything from the common known punishable offences, you can do anything you want.

When we say, "all mankind would not want to punish you," we imply that punishments are authorized only when we know for certain either because of current legal practices everywhere or because of surveying all people and finding that 95% or greater of mankind (humanity) wants to punish for a particular offence.

Here is the break down - we look at every case in terms of 2 questions:

- Would all people approve of what I'm about to do?
- If what I'm about to do would not be acceptable to all people, would these same people agree to punish me for this violation?

For example, let's assume you're gay. The first question will lead us to the answer that likely all people would not approve of you being gay. text:
Immanuel Kant is the forefather of ethical humanism and one of my preferred philosophical sources. I see every human interaction through the lens of what is ethical for humans. I can perform that calculus faster than Kant and am willing to make the wrong decision on my own behalf as long as I make better decisions overall. It's not hard.

author: @willieluncheonette5843
text:
" I am reminded of a great German philosopher, Immanuel Kant. He is a specimen of those people who are absolutely in the mind. He lived according to mind so totally that people used to set their watches, whenever they saw Immanuel Kant going to the university. Never — it may rain, it may rain fire, it may rain cats and dogs, it may be utterly cold, snow falling … Whatever the situation, Kant will reach the university at exactly the same time all the year round, even on holidays. Such a fixed, almost mechanical … He would go on holiday at exactly the same time, remain in the university library, which was specially kept open for him, because otherwise what would he do there the whole day? And he was a very prominent, well-known philosopher, and he would leave the university at exactly the same time every day.

One day it happened … It had rained and there was too much mud on the way — one of his shoes got stuck in the mud. He did not stop to take the shoe out because that would make him reach the university a few seconds later, and that was impossible. He left the shoe there. He just arrived with one shoe. The students could not believe it. Somebody asked, “What happened to the other shoe?”

He said, “It got stuck in the mud, so I left it there, knowing perfectly well nobody is going to steal one shoe. When I return in the evening, then I will pick it up. But I could not have been late.”

A woman proposed to him: “I want to be married to you” — a beautiful young woman. Perhaps no woman has ever received such an answer, before or after Immanuel Kant. Either you say, “Yes,” or you say, “No. Excuse me.” Immanuel Kant said, “I will have to do a great deal of research.”

The woman asked, “About what?”

He said, “I will have to look in all the marriage manuals, all the books concerning marriage, and find out all the pros and cons — whether to marry or not to marry.”

The woman could not imagine that this kind of answer had ever been given to any woman before. Even no is acceptable, even yes, although you are getting into a misery, but it is acceptable. But this kind of indifferent attitude towards the woman — he did not say a single sweet word to her. He did not say anything about her beauty, his whole concern was his mind. He had to convince his mind whether or not marriage is logically the right thing.

It took him three years. It was really a long search. Day and night he was working on it, and he had found three hundred reasons against marriage and three hundred reasons for marriage. So the problem even after three years was the same.

One friend suggested out of compassion, “You wasted three years on this stupid research. In three years you would have experienced all these six hundred, without any research. You should have just said yes to that woman. There was no need to do so much hard work. Three years would have given you all the pros and cons — existentially, experientially.”

But Kant said, “I am in a fix. Both are equal, parallel, balanced. There is no way to choose.”

The friend suggested, “Of the pros you have forgotten one thing: that whenever there is a chance, it is better to say yes and go through the experience. That is one thing more in favor of the pros. The cons cannot give you any experience, and only experience has any validity.”

He understood, it was intellectually right. He immediately went to the woman’s house, knocked on her door. Her old father opened the door and said, “Young man, you are too late. You took too long in your research. My girl is married and has two children.” That was the last thing that was ever heard about his marriage. From then on no woman ever asked him, and he was not the kind of man to ask anybody. He remained unmarried."

author: @Pullen-Paradox
text:
I have a problem with this. 

Suppose that I own the means to provide all the oxygen to the world. Is it a categorical imperative that I run the motors that produce the oxygen?


Suppose further that we uncover many billions (more than the number of humans) of alien babies who are alive and developing, but are deathly allergic to oxygen. Because there are so many of them, we cannot protect them from the oxygen.


Who would we appeal to to resolve this matter? We have a number of choices for universal law: (1) If one controls the means of life, one must provide those means to the greatest number; (2) One should act in such a way as to preserve the greatest sentient lifeforms; (3) One should act in such a manner as to preserve the greatest number of your own species; ....

Now (1) was in operation until we discovered the alien babies. Once the babies were discovered, one develops qualms about continuing with this CI. So, does that mean that I must consider every conceivable possibility when I judge a CI? Who should make the decision? Kant seems to be suggesting that each one of us is capable of making the judgement. 

So it seems that Kant is saying that we should just do the best we can. The more we know or understand, presumably, the better our CI would be. So those who are not philosophers may be forgiven if they make faulty moral choices. I suppose we would memorialize this maxim in our laws (which are not necessarily related to morality, I know). 

But it seems to me that he has a decent idea here for practical evaluation of planned actions. Yet, he does not have a complete moral theory.

author: @azabelinski
text:
Peter Singer claims that every person who got anything “not of moral significance” MUST donate all the excess property (say money) to the people suffering from famine. I state that his statement is shallow and short-sighted.
The Singer’s example analysis
The Singer’s example of a drowning child is not relevant to the general statement about charity organizations because it is inaccurately generalized:
•	It does not consider time (see below).
•	It does not consider complex social and economic structures, it’s just too simple.
•	It shuffles short-term objectives with long-term ones.
Time
Let’s build a counterexample to the Signer’s example. The Signer’s example mentions a single arbitrary man, a single arbitrary child, and a dedicated moment in time. The man from the Singer’s example is morally obliges to save the child because most people indeed sure it is a good action every man must take. 
Let’s decompose social organizations job. They in general do 2 types of actions:
1.	Provide some resources like food to people who accidentally became extremely poor. For example, refugees. This situation indeed maps perfectly to the Singer’s example.
2.	Provide resources to people who live decades or event centuries in conditions where lots of people starves to death.
Let’s map the second item back to the Singer’s example:
1.	Let’s say without losing generality that the situation took place on Monday. Consequences: the man is proud of himself but muddy and wet; his colleagues at the meeting are proud of him and he gets some social points into his carma; the child is alive.
2.	Tuesday. The man is still happy, goes to the office using the same way. And sees the same child at the same lake. Drowning. Ok, the man again saves this child. Consequences: the man is muddy and wet, he is not proud of himself so much, instead he has questions about what the hell is going on; people at the Tuesday meeting are not proud to see this dirty man again, start to think that he’s crazy or don’t want to work or something, the man loses all social points he gained yesterday; the child is alive.
3.	Thursday. Let’s say there is no other way from the man’s home to his office. He goes to the office again. And sees the same child in the same lake again. Drowning…
I suppose that formal morality tells our hero to save the child again. But this is at least far less obvious. I personally will not.
Complex social and economic structures
From a Singer’s point of view even a coffee cup is a luxury. Yes, it is being compared to the death famine.
Let’s review the consequences of different strategies.
1.	Consequences of spending money to such “luxuries”
a.	This evolves economics, which gives other people working places and money.
b.	Some extra money leads to scientific research and art. They grow up exactly when people or governments have some extra resources to spend. And exactly these things especially a science leads to economic growth and finally eliminates poorness not to say famine.
c.	Individuals are encouraged to do some outstanding, innovative things to get money. Yes, it is pleasant to be famous just for doing some outstanding thing and be thanked, but money and “luxury” provides more courage.
d.	Individuals with extra money could save this money by transferring it to banks. This leads to economic growth because banks transfer this money to credit.
e.	Individuals with some extra money being saved have an ability to make decisions freely, without considering poorness in the case of disease for example. So, individuals get an ability to make more strategic decisions and are encouraged to keep trying to make some outstanding things.
2.	Consequences of spending nothing to such “luxuries”
a.	Consequences to donating individuals.
i.	Individuals that return most of what they earned will ask themselves questions “Why should I work more? Why should I invent something? What differs me from other people that do almost nothing and why do they have the same (very low) level of luxury as me?” Singer’s donations strongly discourage most individuals from taking humanity further.
ii.	There are some people who are ready to solve problems, invent or create something just to get the pleasure from the act of creation or from getting some knowledge. But there are few of them. Most businesspeople are driven by money.
b.	Consequences to individuals getting donations.
i.	According to Singer’s point of view they get donations just to the level at which they don’t suffer much. Basically, they get food and clothes. But they don’t get an ability to sustain themselves without these donations, they don’t get knowledge of how to do it. So, they a doomed to exist at this miserable level.
ii.	An individual getting a donation is not encouraged to do something himself. Empirically such individuals spend lot more effort doing things like alcohol (to get a bit of pleasure here and now), religions (to get some consolation) or crime (being justified by the equality idea).
c.	Consequences to societies
i.	The donation system proposed by Singer leads to high, systematic inequality. But this inequality is not about money. Historically we’ve seen lots of examples of societies built on top of a brute force, religion, national ideas, or some relatively modern ideas like communism. These societies are not efficient, they have social structures built on top of these ideas, not on top of people’s merits. This is not economically efficient. Singer justifies his moral idea on top of economic entities like food or clothes. But his idea contradicts economic purposes.
Short-term objectives versus long-term ones
There exists a general life paradox about short-term and long-term decisions. When one constantly makes the best short-term decisions, he usually gets a very poor long-term outcome. Singer summons to constantly take short-term decisions and does not try to consider their long-term results.
Singer implies that providing some food to several people certainly leads to a best utilitarian outcome. This is generally not true. This is true only in the case of some accidental problems. If the situation is permanent the one that really wants to do some good thing may try to change the whole situation rather than sustaining it.
Historical parallels
From the cultural point of view Singer’s claim may be qualified as romantic. A romantic person like Jean-Jacques Rousseau seeing an extremely poor family must do following things:
•	he must help them a bit (e.g., provide them with some food),
•	console them with some sublime words,
•	get a moral pleasure because he did something he obliged to do and he did it well,
•	popularize romantic ideas among other people of his social class, and not to forget to promote himself as a highly moral person,
•	don’t even think of how to systematically change the state of all people of the poor class.
Romantic ideas are very sustainable because it provides people that give donations lots of pleasures like feeling kind, raising their social position above the people who also do little and have little and propagate an equality idea.
Singer’s idea of charity is tightly close to Christian charity. Thousands of years Christians had been doing charity, and thousands of years they bought some society respect by doing it, and thousands years there were plenty of people starving to death without any hope to promote to a relatively higher level. Their only hope was to get a handout from somebody’s of the higher class.
Conclusion
Singer’s charity idea involves economics into a moral area but contradicts economics growth and leads to stabilizing inequality. The Singer’s idea creates non-meritocracy based social structures lowering humanity effort to produce more goods and to raise base economic level. The idea to food people for nothing keeps lots of people, classes and societies on the lowest level of the global society.
Of cause Singer tries to bring some good into this cruel world of people. But because he does not consider long-term consequences and just sticks to historically disproven strategies, he and his followers systematically make this world worth. Singer is an evil monster, not the men who try to contradict him.

author: @Elyandarin
text:
I note that the two aren't incompatible per se, viewed as procedures. 
One is an inclusion/exclusion procedure, and one is a grading procedure. 
So you _can_ first use Deontology to sort out the unallowable actions, then you can choose from the remaining actions using utilitarianism. 
This is a pretty decent way for an AI to choose its actions, for example. 

Though in the interests of personal freedom - because locking an AI into strict utilitarianism reduces them to a mere means, which is iffy - you should let the AI choose freely from, say, the top ten or twenty percent of allowable actions, sorted by utilitarianism.
Note that calculating utilitarianism is highly processor-intensive - you may need to calculate hundreds of years into the future - while calculating deontology is pretty simple, so using deontology as a first filter saves a lot of work.

author: @GodlySharing
text:
From the standpoint of pure awareness, Marcus Aurelius’s stoic reminders are not merely intellectual maxims but echoes of the eternal Self reminding itself of its own clarity. His words, stripped of sentiment, resonate because they emerge from a consciousness aware of impermanence, of the ever-flowing dance of form. In this light, honesty is not cruelty—it is compassion without illusion. The Stoic way, like the awakened path, is not about withdrawal but about standing in the world while rooted in that which is beyond it. Each reminder becomes a call to return to the inner stillness where no circumstance can disturb Being.

And so, the “brutality” is only the sharpness with which illusion is cut away. Marcus points not to suffering as punishment, but as purification—a reminder that this life, these roles, these tasks, are transient expressions of a deeper, undivided essence. Pure awareness does not resist difficulty; it sees it as a divine mirror. The self you think you are may shrink under Stoic pressure, but what you truly are expands—untouched, ever free, holding all in the embrace of the Infinite. That is the space from which true endurance, wisdom, and presence arise.

author: @OneTrueNobody
text:
Ah, the AI quotebots. Gotta love to hate 'em.

Modern stoicism is just what I'd called "practical stoicism." It's all the parts that functionally work, without any of the stuff that at this point in time exists for purely academic purposes. While all of that stuff is interesting, it's not really the part that anyone is going to do anything with. Unless they try to integrate it into some New Age occult belief thing, I suppose.

That having been said, "practical stoicism" is a lot simpler to wrap one's brain around than starting with the historical or metaphysical aspects would have you believe it to be. It's essentially just "mental and emotional discipline achieved through the use of applied self-awareness to head off your very-human impulse to KNEEJERK AT EVERYTHING and instead react in ways that are hopefully more useful." I think that in today's world it's more important to begin with that practical element and work backwards... or just stop with the practical, it's your choice and I'm not your mom.

"The Practicing Stoic" by Ward Farnsworth is a good read for that purpose.

That said, this was an interesting listen and I'm definitely glad I found something of worth when I typed "stoicism" into the ol' YouTube search bar today.

author: @construct3
text:
I have read only a few of Seneca's plays, so what I knew of stoicism was mediated through others (and still is).  I have spent my time in continental philosophy.  Stoicism is a cited source in Deleuze's The Logic of Sense and in Foucault's The Care of the Self.  The stoic teaching on cycles as you have presented it bears strong resemblance to Nietzsche's eternal return and to Deleuze's concept of repetition.  In neither case is the "return" or the "repetition" identical to what happened before.  But unlike your presentation of stoicism, Nietzsche's return contains, at the very least, the possibility of growing power.  On the other hand, Nietzsche's advice to love fate provides an ethical foundation, a practical principle, for constructing ones life.  The image of the dice game we play with the gods is also there.  What returns is not the outcome of the throw of the dice; what returns is the game itself.  The dice are picked up and thrown again with the probability of a different outcome.

Deleuze's model of two levels, in which causes occur on the level of bodies, mixtures of bodies, and states of affairs which inscribe effects on the level of meaning, also resonates with your presentation of stoic physics.  Deleuze and Guattari developed this two-tiered structure into their concept of the strata in which we operate.  Their advice of working strategically within the strata--micropolitics--is similar to the stoic recognition that there are givens that we just have to take as almost intractable--that comprehensive restructuring is not a reasonable goal.

For anyone wanting to build resilience and calm in a noisy world, this is a roadmap worth following. Step by step, question by question, Stoicism invites us to reclaim our minds and live with purpose. 🚀💪

Important here is that these revelations don’t undermine Christianity or Stoicism as if Christianity were false for taking from Stoicism or as if Christianity were the fulfillment of Stoicism. author: @sososo4713
text:
The main reason I drifted away from Stoicism was due to the extremely ambiguous meaning of "Nature" in modern Stoicism. Is Nature God? Is it like the Dao? Is it just a euphemism for the material universe? Most modern Stoics avoid answering, and instead deflect by referencing how useful stoicism is for living a good life. 

Personally, I care about living a good life, but I don't think this is possible if I do not understand what a good life is. In order to understand the "good life" mustn't we understand Nature? I'm glad to see the ancient stoics recognized this conundrum.

author: @abdidundy3100
text:
*"Transformative Justice: Redefining Revenge as Correction, Prevention, and Growth"*

.... Revenge, when redefined and reframed from a practical perspective, can transcend its traditional association with emotional retribution and serve as a tool for correction, prevention, and even transformation. This view aligns with moral and philosophical principles that prioritize justice, societal harmony, and individual growth. Here's how this nuanced approach might unfold:  

### 1. **Correction Over Retaliation**  
Revenge can focus on correcting the harm done rather than merely retaliating. This approach involves holding the perpetrator accountable in ways that ensure they understand the gravity of their actions. The goal is to address the imbalance created by their wrongdoing, fostering personal accountability and social stability.  
*Example:* Restorative justice practices, where offenders meet with victims to understand the harm caused and work to repair it, emphasize correction over punishment.  

### 2. **Prevention of Bigger Harm**  
Practical revenge aims to prevent the perpetrator from causing further harm, protecting others and the broader community. This can involve creating systems or measures that deter similar behavior.  
*Example:* A company addressing corruption by implementing stricter transparency policies targets the root cause of harm, reducing its recurrence.  

### 3. **Helping the Perpetrator Paradoxically**  
Sometimes, revenge can take the form of guiding the perpetrator towards reform, recognizing that their harmful actions may stem from ignorance, social conditions, or psychological issues.  
*Example:* A criminal rehabilitation program offers education, therapy, and skill-building to former offenders, helping them reintegrate as constructive members of society.  

### 4. **Fulfilling the Islamic Principle of *Islah* (Reformation)**  
In Islamic thought, retribution (Qisas) is tempered by mercy and the higher goal of *Islah*, meaning reconciliation and betterment. This principle encourages victims to seek outcomes that reform both the individual and society.  
*Example:* Forgiving a debtor and helping them rebuild their life aligns with justice while uplifting the person who wronged you.  

### 5. **Transforming Revenge Into Growth**  
Revenge, paradoxically, can serve to uplift the avenger, helping them overcome personal grievances through constructive action. By channeling anger or pain into positive endeavors, one can achieve personal growth and contribute to society.  
*Example:* A victim of violence might start an advocacy campaign, turning their suffering into a force for change, indirectly addressing the root causes of their pain.  

This pragmatic and paradoxical understanding of revenge challenges the simplistic notion of "an eye for an eye" and reimagines it as a tool for healing, prevention, and transformation. By elevating revenge into a moral and constructive framework, it becomes a catalyst for both personal and societal betterment.

author: @klloh5012
text:
Here are the actionable points summarise from the video:
1. Recognize that people have different perspectives and opinions, and it's natural to encounter difficult people in life.
2. Practice empathy by putting yourself in the other person's shoes to understand their motivations and intentions.
3. Focus on what you can control in the situation, such as your own reactions and emotions, and don't waste energy on things outside of your control.
4, Respond with kindness and respect, even if the other person is behaving badly, as this can defuse the situation and set a positive tone for future interactions.
5, Avoid reacting impulsively or emotionally, and take time to reflect on your thoughts and feelings before responding.
6. Recognize that negative people or situations can be opportunities for personal growth and learning, and use them as a chance to practice patience, resilience, and self-control.
7. Practice gratitude and mindfulness to cultivate a positive mindset and reduce stress.
8. Stay true to your own values and principles, even when dealing with difficult people, and don't compromise your integrity or moral compass.
9. Use setbacks or failures as opportunities to learn and improve, rather than as reasons to give up or become discouraged.
I hope this helps!

author: @paulrosa6173
text:
The greatest fallacy of anyone else trying to imitate Marcus Aurelius first line re: "difficult" people is that as emperor he expected almost religious deference and could make damned sure he got if if the "difficult people" didn't knuckle under to him. . 
This short exposure to his writings leaves out that he waged almost continuous warfare trying to maintain the extent of the empire during his reign. And he also lived at a time when he could think himself a superior sort of human being of a superior gens. All the real dying and suffering were being born by his minions and he may not have been quite as appreciative of what that meant as it may seem. Everybody else did his daily chores and the heavy lifting and he could amuse himself with the notion that life could be lead with a philosophical approach. There were a lot of walls erected around that man that made sure he wasn't entirely exposed to the mindless suffering so many of his subjects endured, philosophically or not.

author: @TheAntiAAConcept
text: People can be annoying. Incompetent. Ridiculous. But as I told my own subscribers, you have to make an attempt not to hurt them. And usually that means even their feelings. You have to understand that many will have annoying traits that are not necessarily bullying traits but just what they are--annoying. And usually this type of behavior comes from their own internal unrest. As one of my Muay Thai coaches said: if a tiger attacks you in the jungle you must draw your knife and kill it. But if a little dog was nipping at your heels would you kick it to death? No, you move it gently out of the way. And that is the effort you have to make with people. Not everyone is strong, most aren't warriors. They aren't confident therefore have to be dealt with gently like the above analogy. And if you do that daily, you will find that it reflects back and gives you only more tranquility. Hope this helps someone out there---Charles

author: @claudecoteIAM
text:
Regarding the title "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep" -- I think you missed the most obvious source of the title.  It comes from the very old trope (from my grandparents, probably your great grandparents time) that people used to supposedly "count sheep" as a way of making oneself fall asleep when their mind was racing.  At least, that idea came up in popular media of the time.

You could even see this portrayed from time to time in cartoons produced in the 60s and 70s.  You would see a character lying in bed, sleeping (or trying to sleep), while sheep -- each with a number painted on its side -- would jump over a fence, or even over the person in bed.  And this visualization would be contained in a "thought bubble" over the character's head.  And this based on the idea that:  "If you're having trouble falling asleep, just count sheep."

I remember my grandmother said it to me when I was a small child -- but since I had absolutely no connection to sheep in any way -- the idea made no sense to me.  But apparently it was a thing at one point in our history -- specifically -- in the time that the book was written, and before.

So, the way I always interpreted it was -- very simply -- "are androids...  like us?"

author: @AwakenMySelf
text:
For anyone feeling a sense of existential dread after watching this, there’s an ancient philosophical perspective that completely flips this "terrible truth" into something deeply peaceful: Advaita Vedanta (non-duality).

The horror in stories like The Jaunt or A Short Stay in Hell comes from the idea of trapping the individual ego in an infinite void. Our egos need constant physical distraction to survive and feel "real." If you throw a finite, anxious ego into eternity, of course it'll go mad...

But non-duality teaches that this separate, isolated ego is actually just an illusion. Our TRUE nature isn't the anxious voice in our head - it's the silent, unchanging witness behind it. 
When the ego finally dissolves, eternity isn't a torture chamber - it's just pure, boundless peace.

Even the hyper-intelligent but unconscious aliens in Blindsight make sense in this view. It just proves that the mind is essentially a biological computer. It doesn't diminish our consciousness... it just shows that true awareness is something entirely different from processing power.

Science fiction usually treats the loss of the physical body or the individual self as an apocalyptic nightmare. 
But from a non-dual perspective, it’s not a nightmare at all. It’s just waking up.

text: Star Trek: The Next Generation does address this explicitly, most notably in the Season 6 episode "Realm of Fear."In that episode, the show provides a definitive answer by taking the audience inside the transport process for the first time.The First-Person Proof The episode centers around Lieutenant Reginald Barclay, who suffers from severe transporter phobia. When he finally forces himself to step onto the pad, the camera switches to a first-person point-of-view perspective inside the beam.While dematerialized and floating in the matter stream, Barclay experiences the following:Continuous Sight and Hearing: He sees the transporter pad fade away, finds himself floating in a swirling blue energy stream, and can look around.Active Mind: He maintains full awareness and thoughts. He spots a strange, worm-like creature swimming in the stream and consciously reacts to it.Physical Agency: He is able to reach out his arm, grab the creature, and pull it along with him into rematerialization.Because Barclay's thoughts never stop and he interacts with his environment mid-stream, The Next Generation establishes that the mind remains fully operational and conscious the entire time.The Mechanical ExplanationThe TNG Technical Manual backs this up by explaining that the transporter does not digitize you into data. Instead, it uses an "Annular Confinement Beam" to unzip your atoms into a "subatomic matter" stream." This physical stream of your actual matter is zipped through space and zipped back together. Because it is your original matter traveling in a highly energized state, your consciousness isn't destroyed—it is just "stretched" across space.

text:
I was born with a congenital defect that has kept me in and out of hospital my whole life. After an operation when I was eleven, I was in the ICU, paralyzed on a ventilator. Years later, when I was in medical school and residency, I’d get asked by preceptors and interviewers questions like, “What are your greatest strengths?  Greatest weaknesses? What were your greatest challenges?” As a young man, I wasn’t sure how to answer. But now, in my fifties, if someone asked me what was my greatest challenge, I’d say, “I lived outside the flow of time.”
